# On-call handbook for the platform team

This handbook is for everyone on the platform team's on-call rotation, from people about to take their first shift to people who have done it for years and want to check what changed. It describes how the rotation works, what is expected during a shift, how to handle a page, how to run an incident, and how to hand over. It is deliberately practical. The rules here exist because each of them was missing at some point and its absence hurt; where that history is useful, it is mentioned. If something in this handbook is wrong or outdated, fixing it is part of the on-call job.

#### The rotation

##### Shape of a shift

The rotation has a primary and a secondary for each week, from Tuesday at 10:00 to the following Tuesday at 10:00 local time. Handover on a Tuesday morning rather than a Monday was chosen on purpose: Monday is the busiest day for deploys and for leftover weekend issues, and handing over in the middle of it meant the outgoing person left exactly when context was most needed. The primary gets every page first. If the primary does not acknowledge within ten minutes, the page escalates to the secondary, and after another ten minutes to the engineering manager. The secondary is also the person the primary calls for help, and a primary who has been working on an incident for more than an hour must call the secondary, even at night.

###### Compensation and limits

On-call time is compensated according to the company policy, and pages outside working hours are additionally compensated per incident. More important than compensation are the limits. Nobody does more than one primary week in four, nobody is on call during approved leave, and anyone who was paged for more than two hours between midnight and 07:00 starts work late the next day without needing to ask. Before these limits existed, a few experienced people ended up carrying most of the night pages because they resolved them fastest, and two of them left the team within a year. The limits are not negotiable, including by the people they protect, who sometimes try to waive them.

#### Before your shift

##### Access check

The week before your primary shift, run the access check, which verifies that you can do everything on-call might require: log in to every production cluster, read logs and traces, use the deploy tool's rollback, open the database consoles for the platform's own databases, access the secrets store for break-glass credentials, and receive a test page on your phone. Run it with:

```sh
oncall-preflight --role platform-primary
```

The access check exists because of an incident in which the primary was paged at 03:00 for a full disk on a database node, and discovered that their access to the database hosts had expired the week before during a routine access review. They spent forty minutes getting emergency access approved while the disk filled up. Since then, access expiry for on-call roles is aligned with the rotation schedule, and the preflight is mandatory.

###### Read the last handover

Read the handover notes from the last two shifts and look at the open incident follow-ups. Most pages during a shift are related to something that happened in the previous two weeks, and knowing that a particular alert has been flaky, or that a migration is running on a particular cluster, saves a lot of time when the page arrives.

#### Handling a page

##### First five minutes

When a page arrives, acknowledge it immediately, even before you look at it, so that it does not escalate to the secondary while you are opening your laptop. Then open the alert's linked dashboard, not a general dashboard; every alert links to the dashboard of the affected service, which shows its indicators, dependencies and recent changes on one screen. Within the first five minutes, try to answer four questions: what is broken, since when, who is affected, and what changed recently. Write the answers, even if incomplete, into the alert's channel thread. This is not bureaucracy: written notes are what lets the secondary or anyone else join without asking you to repeat everything, and they are the raw material for the postmortem.

###### Deciding whether it is an incident

Not every page is an incident. A page is an incident if users are affected now or will be soon, if data is at risk, or if you need help from anyone outside the rotation. If none of these is true, handle the page, write a short note in the thread and move on. If any of them is true, declare an incident with the incident tool, which creates a dedicated channel, assigns you as incident commander by default and posts a status page draft. Declaring an incident that turns out to be minor costs a few minutes; not declaring one that turns out to be major costs much more, because the coordination structure is missing exactly when it is needed. When in doubt, declare. During the first year of the current process, about a third of declared incidents were later downgraded to minor, and we consider that a healthy ratio.

##### Mitigation before diagnosis

The first goal during an incident is to stop the harm, not to understand it. If a deploy happened shortly before the problem started, roll it back without waiting to confirm that it is the cause; rollback is cheap and quick, and confirming causation can take an hour. If a feature flag was changed, revert it. If one node or zone is misbehaving, take it out of rotation. Diagnosis comes after the bleeding has stopped. New on-call engineers often feel that rolling back without proof is unprofessional, and the opposite is true: in our incident history, rollbacks that turned out to be unnecessary have never caused harm, while delayed rollbacks have extended several incidents by tens of minutes. Example of a rollback with the deploy tool:

```sh
deployctl rollback --service ingress-gateway --to previous --reason "INC-2291 error spike after deploy"
```

New members of the rotation often ask what a typical week actually looks like, and the honest answer is that most weeks are quiet and a few are not, so it helps to describe both. In a quiet week the primary gets perhaps three to five pages, most of them during working hours, and spends the rest of the time on follow-up work from previous shifts: tuning an alert that fired for no good reason, fixing a runbook step that turned out to be wrong, or writing the missing mitigation note for a change that could not be rolled back. The secondary in a quiet week is mostly not involved at all, apart from the handover call and perhaps one consultation. In a busy week, which happens maybe once every two months, there is a real incident with user impact, often at an inconvenient hour, and the primary spends most of a day on it, including the postmortem preparation that follows. The handbook rules about compensation and limits exist mainly for those weeks, and new members should not feel that taking the late start after a night page is a sign of weakness: it is how the rotation stays sustainable over years rather than months. A completely different question that comes up just as often is how to learn the systems well enough to be useful on call. Reading documentation helps, but the most effective way we have found is shadowing: before their first primary week, every new member spends one full week as a third person on the rotation, receiving every page in parallel with the primary, joining every incident channel and asking questions afterwards, without any responsibility for acting. After the shadow week they take a primary week with an experienced secondary who is explicitly asked to be more available than usual. People who skipped the shadow week because of scheduling pressure consistently reported their first primary week as much more stressful, so we no longer allow skipping it. Another practice that helps is the monthly game day, a one-hour session where someone breaks something in the staging environment on purpose, such as filling a disk, killing a database replica or misconfiguring a load balancer, and the current primary diagnoses it with the rest of the team watching. Game days are deliberately low-stakes and are often funny, but they have found real gaps more than once: the most memorable was a game day where nobody could find the dashboard for the message queue cluster, because its link had broken during a migration of the dashboard system weeks earlier and nobody had needed it since. Going back to the quiet weeks, one thing that experienced members do differently is that they use the quiet time to look at the alert history for patterns rather than waiting for the weekly review. An alert that fired four times in a week, each time resolving on its own within five minutes, is easy to miss in the review summary, but it is often an early sign of a capacity problem that will become a real incident a month later. The handbook does not require this, but it is the habit that most clearly separates people who have been on the rotation for years from those who have just joined. We are also experimenting with a short weekly note from the outgoing primary to the whole team, not only to the incoming primary, summarising anything that looked like the beginning of a trend, so that the knowledge does not stay with the two people on the handover call. The first few of these notes have already prompted two capacity tickets that would otherwise have waited for the quarterly planning. There is one more kind of week worth mentioning, which is the week of a large planned change, such as a database migration or a major upgrade of a shared cluster. Those weeks are scheduled with the rotation in mind: the change is announced at least a week ahead, the change author is on standby during and after the change, and the primary for that week is told explicitly what to watch and when to call the author. The rotation does not own planned changes, and the primary should never be the person executing a large change during their shift, because the two roles compete for attention exactly when something goes wrong. If the only person who can execute a change is on call that week, the change moves to another week or the on-call shift is swapped.

###### When rollback is not possible

Some changes cannot be rolled back simply: database migrations that dropped a column, configuration changes to external providers, data that has already been written in a new format. For changes like these, the change itself must come with a documented mitigation, and the deploy tool shows that mitigation note when someone attempts a rollback. If you hit a change without a rollback path and without a mitigation note, call the change author immediately, regardless of the time. That is an explicit expectation for every engineer who ships irreversible changes, and it is in the change process for that reason.

#### Running an incident

##### Roles

For any incident bigger than one person can handle, split the roles. The incident commander coordinates: decides what to try next, makes sure someone is working on each line of investigation, and keeps track of time. The commander does not debug. The communications lead posts status updates to the incident channel every thirty minutes and to the public status page when customers are affected, and handles questions from support and management so that responders are not interrupted. Responders investigate and act. In a small incident, the primary is commander and responder and the secondary handles communications; in a large one, the commander should be someone who is not hands-on, and the primary should hand over the commander role as soon as such a person joins.

###### Status updates

Status updates follow a fixed format: current impact, what we know, what we are doing, and when the next update will be. The last item matters most. A stakeholder who knows that the next update comes in thirty minutes does not ask for one in ten. Updates should be honest about uncertainty: "we do not yet know the cause; we are rolling back the 14:05 deploy as a precaution" is a good update, while silence for an hour followed by a confident root cause is not.

##### Ending an incident

An incident ends when user impact has ended and the system is stable, not when the cause is understood. The commander declares the end in the incident channel, the communications lead posts a resolution on the status page, and the commander assigns a postmortem owner. Postmortems are required for every incident with user impact longer than fifteen minutes or any data loss, and are held within five working days, while memory is fresh. They are blameless: the purpose is to understand how the system allowed the incident, and the document must not name individuals as causes.

###### Talking to other teams

Many platform incidents involve another team's service, either as cause or as victim. When you need another team, page their on-call through the incident tool rather than messaging people you know directly; the tool records who was paged and when, and it respects their escalation policy. Messaging a friend on another team at night bypasses their rotation, puts the burden on someone who may not be on call, and leaves no record for the postmortem. If the other team's on-call does not respond within their escalation window, escalate to their manager through the tool, without guilt.

#### Noise and alert hygiene

A rotation is only sustainable if pages are rare and meaningful. Every page during a shift is recorded with a classification: actionable and urgent, actionable but could have waited, not actionable, or false alarm. At the weekly on-call review, every page that was not actionable and urgent gets a follow-up: tune the alert, change it to a ticket instead of a page, or delete it. Over the last year this review reduced the average number of pages per week from twenty-three to seven, and night pages from about six per week to one or two. The most effective single change was converting alerts on resource saturation, such as CPU and memory, into tickets, and keeping pages only for symptoms that users feel: error rates, latency and data freshness.

###### Flaky alerts

An alert that fires and resolves on its own several times a week trains people to ignore it, and eventually someone ignores it when it is real. Any alert that self-resolves more than three times in a week is automatically flagged in the on-call review, and the default action is to silence it until it is fixed, with a ticket assigned to the owning team. Silencing an alert feels risky, but a flaky alert that everyone ignores already provides no protection; silencing it at least makes that explicit.

#### Handover

At the end of the shift, the outgoing primary writes a handover note and spends fifteen minutes on a call with the incoming primary. The note lists incidents and notable pages with links, anything still in progress, alerts that were flaky, any temporary changes made during the shift that need to be undone, such as silenced alerts, scaled-up resources or manual overrides, and anything the next shift should watch. Temporary changes are the most important item: in a past incident, a manual scale-up made during a shift was never reverted and was forgotten, and when the autoscaler configuration was later changed, the manual override silently prevented it from working, which turned a minor traffic spike into an outage weeks later. Example of the handover template's temporary changes section:

```text
Temporary changes still in place:
- alert "etcd-latency-high" silenced until 2026-03-21 (ticket PLAT-4410)
- ingress-gateway min replicas raised 6 -> 10 (revert after traffic test, owner: secondary)
```

##### After your shift

Take the day after a heavy shift easy if you can, and use some of your next week to do the follow-ups you found: fix the runbook that was wrong, tune the alert that woke you up for nothing, write the missing mitigation note. The rotation gets better only when people who experienced its problems spend time fixing them. The engineering manager tracks on-call follow-ups as part of the team's regular work, not as a side activity, and there is reserved capacity for them in every sprint.

# crontab: почему задача работает руками и молчит по расписанию

Короткий список того, на что я наступал с cron, чтобы не искать заново.

- **Окружение почти пустое.** У cron свой `PATH` (обычно `/usr/bin:/bin`), нет переменных
  из `.bashrc` и `.profile`. Скрипт, который вызывает `node` или `aws` из `/usr/local/bin`,
  падает с «command not found». Решение: абсолютные пути или строка `PATH=...` в начале
  crontab.
- **Знак `%` — перевод строки.** В строке crontab `%` превращается в newline, всё после
  первого `%` уходит на stdin команды. `date +%F` нужно писать как `date +\%F`.
- **Вывод.** stdout и stderr уходят письмом на `MAILTO`; если почта не настроена, вывод
  теряется. Пишите в журнал явно: `... 2>&1 | logger -t backup`.
- **Последняя строка без перевода строки** игнорируется некоторыми реализациями.
- **Наложение запусков.** cron не знает, что прошлый запуск ещё идёт. Оборачиваю в
  `flock -n /run/lock/backup.lock команда`.
- **Файлы в `/etc/cron.d/`** имеют лишнее поле пользователя и не должны содержать точку
  в имени — на Debian `run-parts` пропускает такие файлы.
- **Часовой пояс** — системный; после смены пояса перезапустить сервис cron.

   ###### CPU fallback
   
   When the GPU pool is unavailable or saturated, search falls back to serving without reranking, which costs a few points of relevance but keeps search working. We also built a CPU fallback for the cross-encoder using a quantized int8 version of the model, which runs within the latency budget only for the top twenty results instead of forty. In an exercise where we drained all GPU nodes in one zone during peak, the fallback served that zone's traffic for twenty minutes with a relevance drop that was barely visible in online metrics, which gave us confidence that a GPU outage is an inconvenience and not an emergency.
   
   ##### Model registry hygiene
   
   The registry holds every model version that was ever registered, with its training data reference, evaluation results, export artifacts and the serving configuration it was validated with. Early on, the registry also held about four hundred versions that had never been deployed, because every training run registered its output automatically. We changed registration to an explicit step that requires passing the offline evaluation thresholds and the skew check, and archived versions that have not been served in ninety days. The serving platform refuses to load an archived version without an explicit override, which prevents a configuration mistake from pointing production at a model trained a year ago.
   
   #### Lessons
   
   Most of our serving problems were not about models. They were about cold starts, about features computed in two places, about resource usage that only showed up at full scale, and about the operational differences between frameworks. Standardizing on one model server and one export format removed a whole category of problems. Logging serving-time features removed most of the skew. Shadow mode removed surprises about resource usage. What remains hard is the latency budget: each new model generation is a little bigger than the last, and every quarter we have the same negotiation between the gain in offline metrics and the milliseconds the product teams are willing to give.
2. n:01M6PCQ78FEZJ99B316G3YTZM5 Knowledge/en/long/ml-model-serving-notes › Serving the recommendation and ranking models in production > Rollout of new model versions  [0.57] rev1 · 2026-11-05 · сегодня · ~483 tok
   #### Rollout of new model versions
   
   ##### Shadow, canary, experiment
   
   A new model version goes through three stages. In shadow mode, the server scores every request with both the current and the new version, returns only the current version's scores, and logs both; this verifies latency and error rates under real traffic and lets us compare score distributions without affecting users. In canary mode, a small share of traffic, usually one percent, gets the new version's scores, which verifies that nothing breaks downstream. Finally, an online experiment with a proper split measures the effect on business metrics. A model can be rolled back at any stage by a configuration change that takes effect within a minute, because both versions stay loaded until the experiment concludes.
   
   ###### The incident that added shadow mode
   
   Shadow mode was not part of the original process. It was added after a ranking model version passed offline evaluation and went straight to a canary, where it raised CPU usage on the ranking nodes by about sixty percent because it used four times as many trees as its predecessor. The canary itself was fine at one percent of traffic, but the planned ramp to fifty percent for the experiment would have exhausted the CPU on the ranking nodes during peak hours. Shadow mode now runs for at least twenty-four hours at full traffic before any canary, which surfaces resource usage at production scale before any user sees the new model.
   
   #### Capacity and cost
   
   GPU nodes are the most expensive part of the platform, and the cross-encoder is the only model that uses them. We run it on a pool of GPU nodes sized for peak traffic plus one node of headroom per availability zone. Off-peak, utilization drops to around fifteen percent, and we experimented with scaling the pool down at night. Scaling down works, but scaling up is slow: a new GPU node takes about four minutes to join, including image pull and model warm-up, and morning traffic rises faster than that. We now scale on a schedule that anticipates the morning ramp by thirty minutes, with reactive scaling only as a safety net.

Once the rollback had been applied and resolver latency was normal again, error rates at the gateway stayed elevated for almost twenty minutes, which confused everyone, because the cause had been removed. The reason turned out to be negative caching in the gateway's own resolver library: during the outage it had cached failures for some upstream names, with a negative cache lifetime that came from the zone's SOA record and was set to fifteen minutes years ago, when the internal zones were first created. Every gateway instance kept returning cached failures for those names until the entries expired, and the instances that had been restarted early in the incident were the last to recover. Lowering the negative cache lifetime in the internal zones to thirty seconds was a one-line change, and it is now part of the zone templates, so that the next resolution problem, whatever its cause, heals within half a minute of the fix rather than a quarter of an hour. The resolver supports a per-upstream limit on concurrent queries, which would have contained the damage, but it was not configured. Example of the setting we have now added for every forwarder:

   ```text
       forward-addr: 10.200.0.53
       forward-first: no

   ```

   ##### Timeouts that were too long
   
   The forwarding timeout was set to the software default, which waits several seconds and retries before giving up. For forwarded zones inside our own network, an answer that does not arrive within a few hundred milliseconds is not going to arrive. We lowered the timeout for forwarders and, more importantly, configured the resolvers to cache failures from a forwarder for a short time, so that a dead upstream causes one slow query per interval rather than one per request.
   
   ###### Parallel rollout
   
   The configuration management system applied the change to all twelve resolvers at once. If it had rolled out to one resolver at a time with a health check between them, the first resolver in an affected region would have failed its health check within a minute, and the rollout would have stopped with most of the fleet untouched. The stub resolver on each host would have failed over to the second, healthy resolver. Parallel rollout is a reasonable default for many roles, but for a role whose failure affects everything, it is not.
   
   ###### Rollback latency
   
   The rollback took seventeen minutes from decision to effect, because the configuration management agent on the resolver hosts runs on a thirty-minute schedule and the system does not support forcing an immediate run for a single role without an extra approval step that was not documented in the runbook. The approver for that step was in a meeting. We have since added the resolver role to the list of roles that support an emergency push, with a documented approval path that the incident commander can grant.
   
   #### What went well
   
   Several things worked as intended. The local caching stub on each host meant that names resolved recently continued to work for up to five minutes, which is why the outage was partial rather than total in the first minutes. The gateway's alert fired within four minutes of the change, which is fast. Once the right people were in the channel, the diagnosis took about fifteen minutes, mostly because resolver metrics clearly showed in-flight queries pinned at the maximum.
   
   #### Action items
   
   ##### Completed
   
   - Per-forwarder concurrency limits and short timeouts on all resolvers.
   - Negative caching of forwarder failures for thirty seconds.
   - Resolver role switched to rolling deployment, one instance at a time, with a health check that resolves a set of names from every internal zone and every forwarded zone.
   - Emergency push path documented and tested for the resolver role.
   - The overlapping address range was fully decommissioned and removed from reverse zones.

   The storefront's search and product pages had been getting slower for about eighteen months, slowly enough that no single release looked guilty. Field data showed the 75th percentile Largest Contentful Paint on mobile at 4.1 seconds for product pages and 3.6 seconds for search results, both well above the 2.5 seconds that counts as good, and Interaction to Next Paint on search results was poor on mid-range Android phones. This audit was a six-week effort by two frontend engineers and one platform engineer to find out where the time went and fix the biggest problems. The document lists findings in the order we found them, then the fixes and their measured effect in field data.
   
   #### Method
   
   ##### Lab and field data
   
   Lab measurements, taken with a fixed device profile and network throttling, are reproducible and good for comparing changes, but they do not tell you what real users experience. Field data from real user monitoring tells you what users experience, but it is noisy and slow to react to changes. We used both: lab runs on every candidate fix to decide whether it helped at all, and field data over at least a week after shipping to decide whether it helped users. Our real user monitoring collects the core web vitals with attribution, meaning it records not just the value of each metric but also which element was the largest contentful paint and which interaction was slowest, along with the device class and connection type. That attribution data turned out to be the most useful input of the whole audit.
   
   ###### Segmenting by device
   
   Averages across devices hide almost everything. When we split field data by device class, high-end phones and desktops were already fast; nearly all of the poor experiences came from mid-range and low-end Android devices, which make up about forty percent of our mobile traffic in some regions. Every lab run from then on used a profile that emulated a mid-range Android device with a four-times CPU slowdown, rather than the default profile of a fast laptop.
   
   #### Findings
   
   ##### Largest Contentful Paint on product pages
   
   On product pages the largest contentful element was almost always the main product image. The attribution data broke LCP into four parts: time to first byte, the delay before the image request started, the time to download the image, and the delay between download and rendering. Time to first byte was reasonable at around 600 ms on mobile. The download itself was also reasonable. The large part was the delay before the image request started: on median devices, the browser did not begin downloading the main image until about 1.8 seconds after the response started arriving.

# Serving the recommendation and ranking models in production

These notes cover how the recommendation and search ranking models are served, from the moment a trained model is registered to the moment a request gets scores back. They grew out of a year of operating the serving platform and of several incidents that taught us what matters. The audience is engineers on the ML platform team and data scientists who want to understand what happens to their model after training. Training itself is out of scope. The sections on batching and on model rollout are the most practical; the section on feature skew is the one that explains most of the strange behaviour people report.

#### The models

##### What we serve

There are three model families in production. The candidate retrieval model is a two-tower network that maps users and products into the same embedding space; product embeddings are computed offline and loaded into a vector index, and only the user tower runs online. The ranking model is a gradient-boosted tree ensemble that scores a few hundred candidates per request using about two hundred features. The search reranking model is a small cross-encoder transformer that scores query and product title pairs for the top forty search results. The three have very different serving profiles: the user tower is a small neural network that needs low latency on every page view, the ranking model is CPU-bound and processes hundreds of rows per request, and the cross-encoder is the only one that needs a GPU.

###### Latency budgets

The recommendation widget on the home page has a total budget of 120 ms at the 99th percentile, of which the model calls may use about 60. Search reranking has a budget of 40 ms at the 99th percentile on top of the base search latency. These budgets were negotiated with the product teams and they drive almost every design decision below: if a model does not fit in its budget on the serving hardware, it does not ship, regardless of its offline metrics.

#### Serving architecture

##### Model server

All three families are served by the same model server, which loads models from the model registry, exposes a gRPC endpoint per model version and handles batching, metrics and health checks. Tree ensembles run on CPU nodes through a compiled inference library, and neural models are exported to ONNX and run through ONNX Runtime, on CPU for the user tower and with the CUDA execution provider for the cross-encoder. We standardized on ONNX after a period in which each model was served by its training framework's own server; that worked, but it meant three different sets of operational problems, three different metrics formats and three different ways for a model upgrade to fail. Example of the serving configuration for a model version:

```yaml
model: search-rerank
version: 2026-02-11-a
runtime: onnxruntime
device: cuda
max_batch_size: 64
batch_timeout_ms: 3
intra_op_threads: 2
warmup_requests: 200
```

###### Warm-up

The `warmup_requests` setting turned out to be essential. Without warm-up, the first requests to a newly loaded model were dramatically slower: for the cross-encoder, the first few hundred requests after loading took up to ten times longer than steady state, because the GPU runtime was compiling kernels and allocating memory pools for each new input shape. When a new pod joined the load balancer cold, its first minute of traffic violated the latency budget. The server now replays a set of recorded production requests with a representative spread of input lengths against each model before reporting itself ready, and only then does the pod receive traffic.

##### Batching

Dynamic batching is the main lever for GPU efficiency. Requests for the cross-encoder arrive individually, each with about forty query and title pairs, and the server collects requests for up to three milliseconds or until the batch reaches sixty-four pairs, whichever comes first, then runs one inference call for the whole batch. The batch timeout is a direct trade between latency and throughput. With a timeout of one millisecond, the median batch at peak traffic was about twenty pairs and GPU utilization stayed under thirty percent. With three milliseconds, the median batch reached the maximum of sixty-four at peak, GPU utilization rose to about seventy percent, and the 99th percentile latency increased by only two milliseconds, because the time saved by more efficient batches offset most of the time spent waiting. We settled on three milliseconds after measuring a range of values under replayed peak traffic.

###### Padding and sequence length

Transformers process batches of equal-length sequences, so shorter inputs are padded to the length of the longest input in the batch. Product titles vary from a few tokens to over a hundred, and a batch with one very long title wastes most of its compute on padding for all the others. We introduced length bucketing: the server keeps separate queues for inputs up to 32, 64 and 128 tokens and batches each queue separately. Titles longer than 128 tokens are truncated, which affected less than half a percent of products and had no measurable effect on ranking quality. Bucketing raised throughput per GPU by about forty percent at the same latency.

#### Feature skew

The most frequent source of confusing behaviour is training-serving skew: a feature computed one way in the offline training pipeline and a slightly different way in the online feature service. The model then sees values in production that it never saw in training, and its predictions degrade in ways that are hard to diagnose because nothing is technically broken. In our first year we found skew in about one in five new models, usually only after a disappointing online experiment. One memorable example was a feature for the number of days since the user's last purchase. Offline, it was computed from the order table with the date truncated to midnight in UTC; online, it was computed from a cached user profile with timestamps in the user's local time zone. For users in time zones far from UTC the feature was off by one for part of every day, and since the model had learned a sharp effect around the first day after a purchase, recommendations for those users flickered between two quite different sets during the day.

The latency budgets deserve a longer explanation, because they are the constraint that people outside the team understand least and argue about most. A budget of 60 milliseconds at the 99th percentile for the model calls on the home page sounds generous until you account for everything that has to happen inside it: the request has to cross the network to the model server, wait in the batching queue, have its features fetched from the online feature service, run through the model, and come back. The feature fetch alone takes 8 to 15 milliseconds at the 99th percentile, depending on how many features the model needs, and the network adds two or three more in each direction. That leaves the model itself with something like 30 milliseconds at the tail, and the tail is what matters, because a page that waits for the slowest of several model calls will feel the 99th percentile of each of them on a much larger share of page views than one percent. When the data science team proposed a ranking model with about five hundred features instead of two hundred, the offline metrics were clearly better, but the feature fetch for five hundred features took 31 milliseconds at the 99th percentile on its own, and the model could not fit in what was left. The compromise was to keep the larger model but to precompute the hundred most expensive features per user in a nightly batch job and store them alongside the user embedding, so that the online fetch for those features is a single key lookup rather than a computation. That brought the fetch back to 12 milliseconds and the model shipped a quarter later than planned. A rather different topic that kept coming up in the same discussions was reproducibility of online scores. Product managers would sometimes report that a particular user got strange recommendations, and the team would try to reproduce the scores offline with the same model version, only to get different numbers. The cause was almost always that the features had changed between the time of the request and the time of the investigation: the user had bought something, the product had sold out, or a rating had moved. Since we started logging the full feature vector for a sample of requests, the first question in any such investigation is whether the request is in the sample, and if it is, the scores can be reproduced exactly; if it is not, we can usually only say what the model would score now. We considered logging features for every request, but at our traffic that would be several terabytes per day, and the sample has been enough for every investigation so far, provided that the investigation starts within the seven days for which the feature log is kept. Coming back to latency, the team also learned that the budgets themselves need revisiting. The 60 millisecond budget for the home page was set three years ago, when the page made two model calls in sequence; since then the calls were parallelized and the page itself became faster, so in principle the models could have more time without the user noticing. We measured the effect of artificially adding latency to the recommendation widget on engagement and found no measurable change up to an extra 40 milliseconds at the median, which is now the basis for a request to raise the budget to 80 milliseconds. Whether that request is granted is a product decision, but for the first time it is being argued with data rather than with intuition on both sides. The budget conversation also changed how the data science team evaluates models before proposing them. They now run every candidate through a latency harness that replays recorded production requests against the model server on the same hardware class as production and reports the 99th percentile of the full call, including feature fetch and batching, next to the offline quality metrics. A candidate that misses the budget is either simplified, distilled into a smaller model, or sent back with a note on which features are the most expensive to fetch. The harness has saved a lot of wasted effort: in the last two quarters, three candidates were reworked before anyone spent time on an online experiment, and one of them ended up faster and better after the expensive features were replaced by cheaper precomputed ones.

##### Logging features at serving time

The structural fix is to log the exact feature values used at serving time and to train on those logs rather than recomputing features offline. The serving platform now logs the full feature vector for a sample of requests, one percent for ranking and five percent for search reranking, together with the model version and the scores, into a feature log table. New models are trained on features from that log, joined with outcomes such as clicks and purchases, so the features in training are by construction the same as in serving. The remaining risk is a new feature that has no history in the log yet; for those, a skew check compares the distribution of the offline-computed feature with the logged online values over a week and blocks registration of the model if they differ by more than a threshold.

###### Monitoring feature distributions

In production, the server publishes summary statistics for every feature of every model, such as the share of missing values, the mean and selected quantiles, every five minutes. An alert fires when a feature's distribution moves far from its trailing week. This has caught upstream breakage more than once: the most useful catch was a change in the feature service that started returning a default of zero instead of a missing value for the product rating when the reviews service timed out. Zero is a legitimate rating value for the model, so it treated those products as terribly rated; the share of zeros in that feature jumped from under one percent to about nine percent during a reviews service slowdown, and the alert fired within ten minutes. Example of a feature monitor definition:

```yaml
monitor:
  model: ranking
  feature: product_avg_rating
  stats: [missing_share, zero_share, p50, p95]
  baseline: trailing_7d
  alert_if:
    zero_share: { abs_change_gt: 0.03 }
```

# .gitignore не игнорирует файл, который уже в репозитории

Типичная ситуация: в репозиторий случайно закоммитили `config/local.toml` с паролем к базе,
потом добавили его в `.gitignore`, а git продолжает показывать изменения в нём.

## Почему так

`.gitignore` влияет только на **неотслеживаемые** файлы: решает, показывать ли их в
`git status` и добавлять ли через `git add .`. Если файл уже есть в индексе, правила игнора
к нему не применяются вовсе.

Проверить, почему файл игнорируется или нет:

```bash
git check-ignore -v config/local.toml     # какое правило и из какого файла сработало
git ls-files config/local.toml            # если выводит путь — файл отслеживается
```

## Решение

Убрать файл из индекса, оставив на диске:

```bash
git rm --cached config/local.toml
git commit -m "Перестать отслеживать локальный конфиг"
```

Для каталога — `git rm -r --cached build/`. Чтобы после правки `.gitignore` разом применить
его ко всему репозиторию:

```bash
git rm -r --cached .
git add .
git commit -m "Применить .gitignore"
```

Важно: у коллег после `git pull` этот файл **удалится** с диска, потому что в истории это
выглядит как удаление. Перед пушем предупредить, чтобы сохранили свои копии, и положить в
репозиторий шаблон `config/local.example.toml`.

## Если в файле был секрет

`git rm --cached` убирает файл только из следующих коммитов, в истории он остаётся. Пароль
считаем скомпрометированным и меняем. Вычистить историю можно через `git filter-repo
--invert-paths --path config/local.toml`, но это переписывает все хеши, и всем придётся
переклонировать репозиторий; копии на сервере и в форках так не удаляются.

## Не путать с assume-unchanged и skip-worktree

Иногда хотят, чтобы файл остался в репозитории, но локальные правки в нём не мешали:

```bash
git update-index --skip-worktree config/settings.toml
git update-index --no-skip-worktree config/settings.toml   # вернуть
git ls-files -v | grep '^S'                                 # список таких файлов
```

Это локальная пометка, она не передаётся другим и может слететь при переключении веток, если
файл там отличается. `--assume-unchanged` по документации — оптимизация производительности, а
не способ игнорировать правки; для этой цели правильнее `--skip-worktree`. Надёжнее всего —
шаблон в репозитории и реальный файл в `.gitignore`.

## Глобальный игнор

Мусор конкретного редактора или ОС (`.idea/`, `.DS_Store`, `*.swp`) не тащим в `.gitignore`
проекта, а кладём в личный файл:

```bash
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.config/git/ignore
```

Для игнора только в своей копии репозитория есть `.git/info/exclude`.

# Файл занят: запущенный exe нельзя перезаписать

На Linux можно заменить исполняемый файл, пока программа работает: старый inode живёт, пока
процесс его держит. На Windows загрузчик открывает образ `.exe` и `.dll` без разрешения на
запись и удаление, поэтому любая попытка их перезаписать заканчивается ошибкой.

## Как выглядит

- Компоновщик MSVC: `LINK : fatal error LNK1104: cannot open file 'target\debug\app.exe'`.
- Копирование: `The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another
  process.` — это `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (32).
- Rust/Go/.NET при пересборке: `Access is denied. (os error 5)` при попытке удалить или
  заменить бинарник.
- Обновление утилиты «поверх себя» падает, если она сама и выполняет обновление.

## Кто держит файл

1. Самое частое — забытый экземпляр программы: запущенный в другом терминале сервер,
   отладчик, тестовый процесс, который не завершился.
2. Монитор ресурсов (`resmon`) → вкладка «ЦП» → «Связанные дескрипторы» → поиск по имени файла.
3. Sysinternals Handle: `handle64.exe app.exe` печатает процессы и дескрипторы.
4. PowerShell: `Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -eq 'C:\src\target\debug\app.exe' }` —
   для самого exe этого достаточно.
5. Антивирус или индексатор поиска могут держать только что созданный файл секунду-две;
   повторная попытка через паузу часто помогает.

## Трюк с переименованием

Запущенный exe нельзя удалить или перезаписать, но **можно переименовать** в пределах тома:
загрузчик держит файл, а не имя. На этом построено самообновление:

```powershell
Rename-Item app.exe app.exe.old
Copy-Item new\app.exe app.exe
# app.exe.old удалить при следующем запуске
```

## Как избежать при разработке

- Перед пересборкой останавливать запущенный бинарник; в скриптах — явно
  `Stop-Process -Name app -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`.
- Тесты, запускающие сервер, должны его гарантированно завершать, иначе следующая сборка
  упадёт на линковке.
- Для DLL, которые грузит долгоживущий процесс (IDE, плагины), копировать их во временный
  каталог перед загрузкой (shadow copy), чтобы оригинал оставался свободным.

# Postmortem: internal DNS resolution failure across the production network

On a Tuesday afternoon, internal name resolution failed intermittently across the production network for one hour and seventeen minutes. Services that needed to resolve internal names, which is nearly all of them, saw a mix of timeouts and `SERVFAIL` responses. External traffic was affected because the API gateway could not reliably resolve its upstream services, and roughly forty percent of customer requests failed at the worst point. This is a blameless postmortem: the goal is to understand how the system allowed a routine change to cause a large outage, not to find someone to blame. Times are in UTC and come from the incident channel, resolver metrics and change logs.

#### Summary

A configuration change to the internal resolvers, intended to add a forwarding zone for a newly acquired company's domain, was rolled out to all resolver instances at once. The new forwarding target was reachable from only some of our network segments. When resolvers in the other segments received queries for that zone, they waited for the forwarding target until timeout, and because the resolver software processed forwarded queries on a shared, limited pool of worker threads, slow forwarded queries exhausted the pool and blocked resolution of every other name, including our own internal zones. The change itself affected one obscure zone, but the failure mode turned it into an outage for everything.

#### Background

##### How internal DNS works here

Internal resolution is handled by a fleet of twelve recursive resolvers spread across three regions. Every host is configured with two resolvers from its own region in its resolver configuration, plus a local caching stub that runs on each host. The stub caches answers for up to the record's time to live, with a cap of five minutes, and retries the second resolver if the first does not answer within two seconds. Authoritative data for internal zones lives on a separate set of authoritative servers, and the resolvers forward internal zones to them. Queries for public names are resolved recursively from the root.

###### The forwarding change

After the acquisition, engineers needed to resolve names in the acquired company's private zone, which was served by their own DNS servers inside a VPN tunnel. The tunnel terminated in one of our three regions. The change added a conditional forwarder for that zone to the resolver configuration, pointing at the acquired company's servers. In the region with the tunnel, those servers were reachable and the change worked. In the other two regions there was no route to them at all, so packets to them were silently dropped by the network rather than rejected, and every forwarded query waited for the full forwarding timeout before failing.

#### Timeline

##### Before the incident

The change was reviewed and approved the previous day. The review checked the zone name and the forwarder addresses, and the change was tested by resolving a name in the new zone from a host in the region with the tunnel, which worked. Nobody tested from the other regions, because the change was seen as additive: it added a zone, it did not change anything about existing zones, so the worst case seemed to be that the new zone would not resolve from some places.

##### During the incident

At 14:02 the change was deployed to all twelve resolvers through the configuration management system, which applies changes to all instances of a role in parallel by default. At 14:06 the first alert fired for elevated error rates on the API gateway. At 14:09 the on-call engineer for the gateway started investigating and saw upstream connection failures with name resolution errors in the logs. At 14:15 the incident was declared and the networking on-call joined. At 14:21 resolver metrics showed that the number of in-flight queries on resolvers in two regions was pinned at the configured maximum, and that query latency for all zones had risen from under a millisecond to several seconds. At 14:30, someone noticed in the resolver logs that a large share of the in-flight queries were for the new forwarding zone. At 14:34 the decision was made to roll back the change. The rollback had to go through the same configuration management system, which first had to finish its periodic run on the resolver hosts; the rollback was applied at 14:51. Resolver latency recovered within a minute of the rollback on each host, but services recovered more slowly because many of them had cached negative answers or had connection pools full of failed connections. The incident was declared resolved at 15:19, after error rates on the gateway had been at baseline for fifteen minutes.

###### Why the new zone was queried at all

The obvious question is why our services were querying a zone they had never heard of. The answer turned out to be the corporate laptop agent. Every laptop that connected to the VPN after the acquisition got a search domain list that included the acquired company's domain, and several internal tools, including the deploy tool that engineers ran from their laptops against production, resolved short host names by trying each search domain in turn. Those queries went through jump hosts in all three regions. On top of that, a monitoring agent on production hosts did reverse lookups on peer addresses, and the acquired company's address ranges overlapped with one of our old, partially decommissioned internal ranges, so reverse lookups for addresses in that range were forwarded to the new servers as well. Neither path was large on its own, but together they produced a few hundred queries per second for the forwarded zone in each region, which was more than enough to exhaust the worker pool when each query took several seconds to time out.

#### Contributing factors

It is worth describing in some detail how the investigation actually unfolded inside the incident channel, because the timeline above makes it look more orderly than it was. For the first ten minutes the gateway on-call engineer treated the problem as an upstream outage, because the error messages in the gateway logs said that connections to upstream services had failed, and the gateway does not distinguish in its logs between a refused connection and a connection that never started because the name could not be resolved. The engineer restarted two gateway instances in the hope that they had a bad connection pool, which made things briefly worse, because the restarted instances started with empty caches and had to resolve every upstream name from scratch through resolvers that were already saturated. Only when the networking on-call joined and asked to see the resolver dashboards did anyone look at the resolvers at all, and the dashboards made the situation obvious within a minute: in-flight queries pinned at the configured maximum in two regions, flat at a normal level in the third. From that moment the question was not whether DNS was the problem but why, and that question took another nine minutes to answer, mostly because the resolver logs record queries but not how long each one waited, so it was not immediately visible that the queries for one zone were the slow ones. The engineer who found it did so by sorting the in-flight query list by age, a debug command that only two people on the team knew existed. That command is now in the resolver runbook, near the top, with an example of what a healthy and an unhealthy output look like. A rather different lesson from the same hour concerns communication with customers. The status page was updated twenty-six minutes after the incident was declared, and the first update said that we were investigating elevated error rates on the API, without saying which part of the API or what customers should do. Several large partners told us afterwards that they had opened their own incidents and spent time investigating their own systems, because our first update did not make it clear that the problem was entirely on our side. Our communications lead has since rewritten the templates for the first status update: it now has to state within fifteen minutes whether the problem is believed to be on our side, which customer-visible functions are affected, and whether customers should retry, wait or switch to a fallback. Writing that update requires the incident commander to make a call early with incomplete information, and the template explicitly allows the next update to correct it. Back on the technical side, one more detail from the investigation deserves a note. Once the rollback had been applied and resolver latency was normal again, error rates at the gateway stayed elevated for almost twenty minutes, which confused everyone, because the cause had been removed. The reason turned out to be negative caching in the gateway's own resolver library: during the outage it had cached failures for some upstream names, with a negative cache lifetime that came from the zone's SOA record and was set to fifteen minutes years ago, when the internal zones were first created. Every gateway instance kept returning cached failures for those names until the entries expired, and the instances that had been restarted early in the incident were the last to recover. Lowering the negative cache lifetime in the internal zones to thirty seconds was a one-line change, and it is now part of the zone templates, so that the next resolution problem, whatever its cause, heals within half a minute of the fix rather than a quarter of an hour. Finally, the incident review itself took longer than usual to schedule because people from four teams were involved, and we were tempted to hold it with only the two teams most directly affected. We did not, and it was the right call: the person from the corporate IT team who maintained the VPN configuration was the one who explained why laptops were pushing the acquired company's search domain to everyone, which nobody on the infrastructure side knew, and without that explanation half of the action items would have been aimed at the wrong place.

##### Shared worker pool

The root technical issue is that the resolver software used one shared pool of workers for all queries, with no isolation between forwarded zones and everything else. A slow upstream for one zone could consume all workers. We confirmed this in a test environment by pointing a forwarded zone at a black-hole address and sending fifty queries per second for it: within twenty seconds, resolution of unrelated names on the same resolver started timing out. The resolver supports a per-upstream limit on concurrent queries, which would have contained the damage, but it was not configured. Example of the setting we have now added for every forwarder:

```text
forward-zone:
    name: "acquired.example"
    forward-addr: 10.200.0.53
    forward-first: no
max-forward-concurrency: 32
```

##### Timeouts that were too long

The forwarding timeout was set to the software default, which waits several seconds and retries before giving up. For forwarded zones inside our own network, an answer that does not arrive within a few hundred milliseconds is not going to arrive. We lowered the timeout for forwarders and, more importantly, configured the resolvers to cache failures from a forwarder for a short time, so that a dead upstream causes one slow query per interval rather than one per request.

###### Parallel rollout

The configuration management system applied the change to all twelve resolvers at once. If it had rolled out to one resolver at a time with a health check between them, the first resolver in an affected region would have failed its health check within a minute, and the rollout would have stopped with most of the fleet untouched. The stub resolver on each host would have failed over to the second, healthy resolver. Parallel rollout is a reasonable default for many roles, but for a role whose failure affects everything, it is not.

###### Rollback latency

The rollback took seventeen minutes from decision to effect, because the configuration management agent on the resolver hosts runs on a thirty-minute schedule and the system does not support forcing an immediate run for a single role without an extra approval step that was not documented in the runbook. The approver for that step was in a meeting. We have since added the resolver role to the list of roles that support an emergency push, with a documented approval path that the incident commander can grant.

#### What went well

Several things worked as intended. The local caching stub on each host meant that names resolved recently continued to work for up to five minutes, which is why the outage was partial rather than total in the first minutes. The gateway's alert fired within four minutes of the change, which is fast. Once the right people were in the channel, the diagnosis took about fifteen minutes, mostly because resolver metrics clearly showed in-flight queries pinned at the maximum.

#### Action items

##### Completed

- Per-forwarder concurrency limits and short timeouts on all resolvers.
- Negative caching of forwarder failures for thirty seconds.
- Resolver role switched to rolling deployment, one instance at a time, with a health check that resolves a set of names from every internal zone and every forwarded zone.
- Emergency push path documented and tested for the resolver role.
- The overlapping address range was fully decommissioned and removed from reverse zones.

##### In progress

- Moving forwarded zones for external parties onto a separate resolver pool, so that no third-party DNS server can ever affect resolution of our own zones.
- Changing the laptop VPN configuration so that search domains for acquired companies are only pushed to people who need them.
- Adding a synthetic check that resolves a set of critical internal names from every region every ten seconds, with an alert on latency, not only on failures.

#### Testing the change before rollout

A change like this one needs to be tested from every place that will run it, not only from the place it was written for. We have added a pre-deployment check to the DNS change pipeline: it starts a resolver with the proposed configuration in each region's test network and runs a standard query set against it, including queries for the new zone, for existing internal zones and for public names, and it measures latency as well as correctness. Run the same check by hand before proposing a change:

```sh
dnscheck run --config resolver.conf --regions all --queryset standard,changed-zones
```

The check would have caught this incident: in two of the three regions, queries for the new zone take several seconds, and the check fails any query set where the 99th percentile latency for any zone exceeds 200 ms.

###### Note on stub resolvers

During the incident some services recovered much later than others even after resolvers were healthy. The slowest to recover were services written in a runtime whose default resolver ignores the host's caching stub and queries the configured servers directly, with no caching of its own; these services had also been configured years ago with a single resolver address rather than two, so they had no failover either. We found eleven such services. All have been changed to use the host stub.

#### Lessons

The change looked additive and low-risk, and in isolation it was. The outage came from three properties of the system that had nothing to do with the change: a shared resource with no isolation, timeouts far longer than any useful answer could take, and a rollout mechanism that applied a change everywhere at once. Each of those properties had been present for years without causing trouble, and each of them is the kind of thing that only matters when something else goes wrong. When reviewing changes to shared infrastructure, we now ask not only "what does this change do" but also "what happens to everything else if the new thing is slow or unreachable." The second lesson is about knowing your traffic. Nobody on the team expected production systems to send any queries to the acquired company's zone, and that expectation was the basis for treating the change as safe. A five-minute look at resolver query logs, filtered by the zone name in a test that simply logged queries without forwarding them, would have shown otherwise. We now run new forwarding zones in log-only mode for a day before enabling forwarding, which tells us who queries them and how often before any real dependency is created.

#### Addendum: findings of the follow-up review

Three months after the outage we held a follow-up review. Its purpose was to check whether the action items had actually changed the behaviour of the system, and to look again at the parts of the timeline that the first write-up had explained only partially. The review was run by an engineer from the storage team who had not been involved in the incident, which turned out to be useful: several things that the network team had taken for granted were questioned for the first time.

##### Client retries

The first finding concerned the clients rather than the resolvers. During the outage, query volume at the resolvers rose to almost three times the normal level, and the first write-up attributed this to services restarting and re-resolving everything at startup. Replaying the resolver logs showed a different picture. A checklist written after two separate incidents on build agents. Both times the
application reported `ENOSPC` / "No space left on device", and both times `df -h` showed

Every file, directory and symlink consumes an inode. Ext4 fixes the inode count when the
filesystem is created, so a directory with millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes
while gigabytes remain free.

```sh
df -i /var
```

```sh
sudo du --inodes -x -d 3 /var | sort -n | tail -20
```

garbage collector was disabled in the container image. The second time it was a
`node_modules` cache per build that nobody cleaned.

- delete the files (with millions of entries `rm -rf dir` can be slow; `find dir -type f
  -delete` streams and does not build a huge argument list);
- fix whatever creates them;
- for the long term, recreate the filesystem with more inod

# cmd и bat-файлы: chcp 65001 и кириллица

В классической командной строке `cmd.exe` кодировку вывода задаёт кодовая страница консоли.
Для русской локали по умолчанию это 866 (OEM), а не 1251 и не UTF-8. Посмотреть текущую:

```
chcp
```

Типичная ситуация: bat-файл сохранён редактором в UTF-8, в нём `echo Сборка завершена`, а в
консоли печатается мусор. Решение — первой строкой переключить страницу:

```bat
@echo off
chcp 65001 >nul
echo Сборка завершена
```

Нюансы, на которые наступал:

- Файл сохранять в UTF-8 **без** BOM. Если BOM есть, cmd воспримет его как часть первой
  команды, и `@echo off` не сработает: в консоли появится `'я╗┐@echo' is not recognized` (три байта BOM, показанные в 866).
- `chcp` меняет страницу для всего окна, после завершения bat-файла она остаётся 65001.
  Если дальше запускаются старые утилиты, которые печатают в 866, вернуть: `chcp 866 >nul`.
- Кириллица в путях внутри bat-файла тоже требует правильной страницы, иначе
  «файл не найден».
- Для программ на Python в той же консоли пригодится `set PYTHONUTF8=1`.

`chcp` касается только консоли cmd. В PowerShell кодировку вывода определяют другие
настройки — для него есть отдельная заметка.

# Кодировка в PowerShell: BOM, Out-File, Set-Content и $OutputEncoding

Кодировки в PowerShell ломаются в четырёх местах: как читается сам скрипт `.ps1`, в какой
кодировке пишутся файлы, как PowerShell передаёт текст внешним программам и как он
декодирует их вывод. Это четыре разные настройки, и путать их — главный источник
«кракозябр». Ниже — то, что я выяснил на Windows PowerShell 5.1 и PowerShell 7.

## 1. Чтение скрипта .ps1

Windows PowerShell 5.1 читает скрипт без BOM в системной ANSI-кодировке (для русской
локали — Windows-1251). Если скрипт сохранён в UTF-8 без BOM и в нём есть кириллица в
строках, она превратится в мусор, а иногда скрипт вообще не распарсится, потому что
кириллическая буква «съест» кавычку.

Правило: скрипты, которые могут запускаться в 5.1, сохраняем в **UTF-8 с BOM**. PowerShell 7
читает UTF-8 без BOM корректно, но BOM ему не мешает.

## 2. Запись файлов: `>`, Out-File, Set-Content

Самая неприятная часть — умолчания отличаются у разных командлетов и версий:

| Способ записи | Windows PowerShell 5.1 | PowerShell 7 |
|---|---|---|
| `>` и `>>` | UTF-16 LE с BOM | UTF-8 без BOM |
| `Out-File` | UTF-16 LE с BOM | UTF-8 без BOM |
| `Set-Content` / `Add-Content` | ANSI (системная кодовая страница) | UTF-8 без BOM |
| `-Encoding utf8` | UTF-8 **с** BOM | UTF-8 без BOM |
| `-Encoding utf8NoBOM` | нет такого значения | UTF-8 без BOM |

Типичный инцидент: в 5.1 сделали `git log > log.txt`, а потом Python-скрипт или `grep`
читает файл с нулевыми байтами через каждый символ — это UTF-16. Другой инцидент:
`Set-Content` записал конфиг с кириллицей в 1251, а сервис ждал UTF-8.

Как писать UTF-8 без BOM в 5.1, где такого значения нет:

```powershell
$utf8NoBom = New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($path, $text, $utf8NoBom)
```

Чтобы не указывать кодировку каждый раз, можно задать значения по умолчанию в профиле:

```powershell
$PSDefaultParameterValues['Out-File:Encoding'] = 'utf8'
$PSDefaultParameterValues['Set-Content:Encoding'] = 'utf8'
```

В 5.1 это всё равно даст BOM, но хотя бы не UTF-16 и не ANSI.

## 3. Текст во внешние программы: $OutputEncoding

Переменная `$OutputEncoding` определяет, в какой кодировке PowerShell отдаёт строки в
стандартный ввод внешней программы при конвейере:

```powershell
"привет" | python -c "import sys; print(sys.stdin.read())"
```

В 5.1 по умолчанию это ASCII, и вся кириллица превращается в `?`. Исправление:

```powershell
$OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)
```

## 4. Вывод внешних программ: [Console]::OutputEncoding

Обратное направление — как PowerShell декодирует байты, которые напечатала внешняя
программа (`git`, `cargo`, `node`). Здесь работает `[Console]::OutputEncoding`, по умолчанию
это OEM-кодовая страница консоли (866 для русской локали). Программа пишет UTF-8, PowerShell
читает как 866 — получаем «╨┐╤А╨╕╨▓╨╡╤В».

```powershell
[Console]::OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)
```

Обычно я ставлю обе переменные в профиль (`$PROFILE`) одной строкой:

```powershell
$OutputEncoding = [Console]::OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)
```

## 5. Чтение файлов: Get-Content

Чтение — зеркальная проблема. `Get-Content` в 5.1 без BOM считает файл ANSI-файлом, поэтому
UTF-8 без BOM с кириллицей читается с искажениями, а потом эти искажения записываются
обратно уже «навсегда». Явно указывать:

```powershell
Get-Content .\config.toml -Encoding UTF8 -Raw
```

`-Raw` возвращает одну строку вместо массива строк — удобно для поиска и замены по всему
файлу. В PowerShell 7 умолчание для чтения — UTF-8, BOM распознаётся автоматически.

Типичная «правка конфига на месте», которая ломает кодировку в 5.1:

```powershell
(Get-Content app.toml) -replace 'debug', 'info' | Set-Content app.toml
```

Здесь два умолчания сразу: чтение как ANSI и запись как ANSI. Если файл был в UTF-8,
кириллица в комментариях превращается в мусор. Правильно — указать `-Encoding UTF8` и там,
и там, а если BOM недопустим, писать через `[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText`.

## 6. Где именно запускается скрипт

Одна и та же команда даёт разный результат в зависимости от хоста:

- **Windows Terminal** и **VS Code** умеют показывать UTF-8, но кодировку процесса
  PowerShell не меняют — `[Console]::OutputEncoding` всё равно надо настроить.
- **PowerShell ISE** использует собственный хост, и `[Console]` там почти ни на что не
  влияет. ISE поддерживает только 5.1, для новых скриптов лучше не использовать.
- **Задание планировщика или служба** запускают `powershell.exe` без профиля пользователя
  (часто с `-NoProfile`), и настройки из `$PROFILE` не применяются. Кодировку нужно задавать
  в начале самого скрипта.
- **CI-агенты** перехватывают вывод через канал, а не консоль; результат зависит от того,
  как агент декодирует поток. Надёжнее явно ставить UTF-8 первой строкой скрипта.

## Глобальный вариант

В «Региональных стандартах» есть флажок «Бета-версия: использовать Юникод (UTF-8) для
поддержки языка во всем мире». Он переводит ANSI- и OEM-кодовые страницы системы на 65001.
Многие проблемы исчезают сразу, но старые программы, рассчитанные на 1251, начинают
показывать мусор. На рабочей машине включал, на машинах пользователей — не рекомендую.

## Как быстро понять, что сломалось

- Мусор вида `Ð¿Ñ€Ð¸Ð²ÐµÑ‚` — UTF-8, прочитанный как 1252/1251.
- Мусор вида `╨┐╤А╨╕` — UTF-8, прочитанный как 866: чинится `[Console]::OutputEncoding`.
- Знаки `?` вместо букв — текст прошёл через ASCII: проверить `$OutputEncoding`.
- Нулевые байты между символами, файл в два раза больше — UTF-16 от `>` или `Out-File` в 5.1.
- Посмотреть первые байты: `Format-Hex file.txt | Select-Object -First 1`. `EF BB BF` —
  BOM UTF-8, `FF FE` — UTF-16 LE.

## Перекодировать существующий файл

Файл, который уже записан в UTF-16 или ANSI, можно привести к UTF-8 без BOM так:

```powershell
$text = Get-Content .\log.txt -Raw            # BOM UTF-16 распознаётся автоматически
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText((Resolve-Path .\log.txt), $text,
    [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false))
```

Для файла в 1251 без BOM в 5.1 достаточно `-Encoding Default` при чтении. Путь передаётся
через `Resolve-Path`, потому что методы .NET отсчитывают относительные пути от текущего
каталога процесса, а он не всегда совпадает с текущим каталогом сессии PowerShell.

## Итог

Для 5.1: скрипты — UTF-8 с BOM, запись — всегда с явным `-Encoding`, в профиле — обе
переменные консоли на UTF-8. В PowerShell 7 большинство проблем ушло, но про
`[Console]::OutputEncoding` для вывода внешних программ всё равно надо помнить.

# Фоновые задачи на Windows: службы (sc.exe), планировщик (schtasks), robocopy и icacls

Разбор того, как мы поставили на Windows-сервер ночное зеркалирование каталога данных и
долгоживущий агент. По пути собралась вся типовая обвязка: служба, задание планировщика,
копирование и права на каталоги. Записываю, чтобы в следующий раз не наступать на те же
грабли.

## Когда служба, а когда задание планировщика

| Нужно | Выбор |
|---|---|
| Процесс работает постоянно, перезапускается при падении | служба |
| Запуск по расписанию, отработал и завершился | задание планировщика |
| Запуск при входе конкретного пользователя, с доступом к его рабочему столу | задание планировщика с триггером входа |
| Запуск до входа любого пользователя | служба или задание с `/SC ONSTART` от SYSTEM |

## Службы и sc.exe

### Важная мелочь про PowerShell

В PowerShell `sc` — это псевдоним `Set-Content`, а не управление службами. Команда
`sc create ...` в PowerShell молча создаст файл с именем `create`. Всегда писать `sc.exe`.

### Создание

```
sc.exe create MyAgent binPath= "C:\apps\agent\agent.exe --config C:\apps\agent\agent.toml" start= auto DisplayName= "My Agent"
sc.exe description MyAgent "Фоновый агент синхронизации"
sc.exe start MyAgent
sc.exe query MyAgent
```

Синтаксис `sc.exe` капризный: после `binPath=`, `start=`, `obj=` **обязателен пробел**, а
перед `=` пробела быть не должно. Ошибка в этом месте даёт невнятную справку вместо
создания службы. Путь с пробелами внутри `binPath` нужно заключать в экранированные кавычки:
`binPath= "\"C:\Program Files\agent\agent.exe\" --flag"`.

### Ошибка 1053

```
Error 1053: The service did not respond to the start or control request in a timely fashion.
```

Самая частая причина — в `binPath` указана обычная консольная программа, которая не
реализует протокол диспетчера служб (SCM): она не сообщает о запуске, и через 30 секунд SCM
считает старт неудачным. Варианты:

- реализовать в программе обработчик службы (во многих языках есть библиотеки для этого);
- запускать через обёртку: WinSW или NSSM — они сами разговаривают с SCM и держат дочерний
  процесс, перенаправляя его вывод в лог.

Вторая частая причина — программа падает при старте, потому что служба работает с другим
текущим каталогом (`C:\Windows\System32`) и не находит относительные пути к конфигам.
Всегда передавать абсолютные пути.

### Учётная запись

| Учётная запись | Права |
|---|---|
| `LocalSystem` | полный доступ к машине, в сети выступает как компьютер |
| `NT AUTHORITY\LocalService` | минимальные права, в сети анонимен |
| `NT AUTHORITY\NetworkService` | минимальные права, в сети как компьютер |
| виртуальная `NT SERVICE\MyAgent` | своя изолированная учётная запись службы |

Задать: `sc.exe config MyAgent obj= "NT AUTHORITY\LocalService"`. Мы используем
виртуальную учётную запись службы и выдаём ей права точечно через `icacls` (ниже).

### Перезапуск при падении

```
sc.exe failure MyAgent reset= 86400 actions= restart/5000/restart/5000/restart/60000
sc.exe qfailure MyAgent
```

Счётчик сбоев сбрасывается через сутки (`reset=` в секундах), первые два перезапуска — через
5 секунд, дальше через минуту.

Удаление: `sc.exe stop MyAgent` и `sc.exe delete MyAgent`. Если оснастка `services.msc`
открыта, служба помечается на удаление и исчезает только после закрытия оснастки.

## Планировщик и schtasks

```
schtasks /Create /TN "Backup\NightlyMirror" /TR "C:\apps\backup\mirror.cmd" /SC DAILY /ST 02:30 /RU SYSTEM /RL HIGHEST
schtasks /Query /TN "Backup\NightlyMirror" /V /FO LIST
schtasks /Run /TN "Backup\NightlyMirror"
schtasks /Delete /TN "Backup\NightlyMirror" /F
```

- `/RU SYSTEM` — задание работает без входа пользователя и без пароля.
- Если нужен конкретный пользователь, но без интерактивного входа, в графическом интерфейсе
  это флажок «Выполнять для всех пользователей»; через `schtasks` — `/RU user /RP *`.
- `/TN` с обратным слешем кладёт задание в папку библиотеки планировщика — удобно
  группировать

Совсем отдельная тема, которая всплыла на тех же обсуждениях, — кто имеет право начинать восстановление в продуктовом окружении. До этого решение принимал дежурный инженер самостоятельно, и это выглядело разумным, пока кто-то не спросил, что будет, если дежурный ошибётся и восстановит базу поверх живых данных, приняв временный сбой репликации за порчу. Мы ввели правило двух ключей: восстановление продуктовой базы на место текущей требует подтверждения второго человека из короткого списка, а восстановление на отдельный сервер для извлечения данных дежурный по-прежнему делает сам.
